metadata.title: Spokane & Spokane County — Public Record Index
metadata.subtitle: An annotated source index on regional politics, extremism, and public safety
metadata.methodology: This index was originally compiled August 9-10, 2026 from publicly available reporting, then expanded across several later sessions with additional entries located via web research and organized into the same format: original one- or two-sentence summaries (never excerpted text), with primary, opinion, and advocacy sources labeled distinctly from independent journalism. As with any research aid, verify anything you plan to rely on against the linked source directly, particularly for entries involving ongoing litigation or unresolved investigations. A small number of entries could not be independently verified due to access restrictions and are noted as such in the webpage's delivery notes rather than included here.

source.title: Washington Rep. Matt Shea engaged in domestic terrorism against U.S., says state House report
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Reports that the independent investigation tied the Spokane Valley Republican to several armed militias and found he used his standing in the Patriot Movement to dispatch militia members to standoffs with government officials.

source.title: Rep. Matt Shea expelled from GOP caucus after investigation finds he engaged in domestic terrorism
source.section: Matt Shea

source.title: Republican Matt Shea ‘participated in act of domestic terrorism’, says report
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: The Guardian, whose own reporting helped trigger the House inquiry, covers the report's conclusion that Shea was likely to keep planning conflicts carrying a risk of bloodshed, and that he met four times with occupation leader Ammon Bundy before the 2016 Malheur refuge takeover.

source.title: Secret chats involving Republican lawmaker reveal fresh evidence of plots and paranoia

source.title: Matt Shea, Washington state lawmaker accused of “domestic terrorism,” refuses to resign

source.title: Death of Otto Zehm

source.title: A complaint that Spokane Police were obstructing the ombudsman's work turns up nothing
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: A city-commissioned investigation clears SPD of obstructing the civilian oversight commission's work; the commission chair and the ombudsman himself dispute the finding's thoroughness.

source.title: Why a dispute between Spokane police and the civilian ombudsman is at a standstill
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Describes a years-long standoff over whether the ombudsman's investigative authority should be resolved through Police Guild contract talks rather than city charter.

source.title: As the Spokane Police Guild negotiates a new contract, the police ombudsman is feeling the union push back
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Ombudsman Bart Logue describes what he calls the Police Guild's resistance to transparency with his office, employees, and the volunteer citizen commission overseeing it.

source.title: Spokane Police Guild eyes long-overdue contract; City Council has questions
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Reports that a contract negotiated under Mayor Woodward's administration did not grant the ombudsman the full independent-investigation authority that voters approved by charter amendment in 2013.

source.title: Contract raises questions for community nonprofit Spokane COPS
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Investigation finds the city-funded community-policing nonprofit employed an officer on the “Brady List” — for lying to cover up the killing of Otto Zehm — and had a volunteer with extremist ties.

source.title: Spokane fails a basic public records test 24% of the time. An audit and new hire aims to improve
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Citywide (not SPD-specific) audit finds Spokane frequently falls short of obligations under Washington's Public Records Act, a law that governs release of police reports and misconduct records.

source.title: Ryan Holyk, teen bicyclist hit by officer, dies in hospital
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Ryan Holyk, 15, died after being struck while riding his bike across Sprague Avenue in Spokane Valley on May 23; the Spokane County deputy who hit him, responding to back up another deputy, was driving roughly 70 mph in a 35 mph zone without lights or siren.

source.title: [UPDATED] Sheriff's Office admits deputy's SUV hit Spokane Valley teen Ryan Holyk
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: After two years of investigations concluding the patrol SUV never made contact, an independent forensic analyst reverses course after matching a hat imprint and Holyk's DNA on the vehicle's bumper, finding it did strike him — contradicting the deputy's own initial radio call (“I hit a pedestrian”) after later denying it.

source.title: Protesters demand Ryan Holyk investigation reopen
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: After the county prosecutor declined to charge the deputy, protesters ask the DOJ and FBI to reopen the investigation; reports note the deputy was traveling over 70 mph without emergency lights when he narrowly missed or struck Holyk.

source.title: Spokane County settles case with family of Ryan Holyk
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Spokane County reaches a settlement with Holyk's family shortly before their civil wrongful-death suit was set to go to trial.

source.title: Wrongful death suits against cities are evolving. After a landmark $4 million settlement, will Spokane Police Department policy change with them?
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Recounts the January 2019 killing of David Novak, shot by officers who mistook the sound of him hitting his own pickup with a baseball bat for gunfire; no gun was found, and the county prosecutor cleared the officers of wrongdoing.

source.title: City of Spokane considering settlement to family of man shot by police
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: The city considers a $250,000 settlement with the family of Peterson Kamo, a 23-year-old Marshallese man shot six times by officers in January 2022 after they say he held a knife to his 2-year-old nephew's throat during a domestic-dispute call; prosecutors cleared the officers.

source.title: Spokane agrees to $3.7 million settlement with children of Robert Bradley, who police shot and killed in 2022
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: The city's second-largest police-shooting settlement ever; Bradley, who was hard of hearing, was shot within seconds as officers arrived to serve a protection order while he unloaded camping gear and guns from his van. A Human Rights Commission member asked whether the city would keep paying out for “the same flawed training.”

source.title: City to pay $3.6M settlement to family of man shot and killed by Spokane police in 2022
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Additional coverage of the Bradley settlement, including bodycam footage showing officers shooting him within seconds of shouting for him to show his hands.

source.title: More to Every Story: The cost of deadly police shooting lawsuits in Spokane
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: An attorney representing the family of Kerry Jones-Hilburg — shot and killed by SPD officers inside a Walmart in December 2023 — puts the city on notice of a planned $50 million lawsuit; the same attorney represented the Bradley estate and a third family from a December 2024 shooting death.

source.title: Spokane police went the entirety of 2025 without shooting and killing someone. The last time was 17 years ago
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: Statistical retrospective noting three fatal police shootings in 2023 and two in one day in 2024, and Mayor Lisa Brown's statement calling the earlier wave of shootings “tragic for everyone involved.”

source.title: No charges for nine Spokane Police officers involved in 2024 shooting that left one man dead
source.section: Spokane Police Department
source.description: The county prosecutor declines to charge nine officers in the fatal shooting of Craig Anglisano, a man reportedly in mental health crisis, after a roughly two-hour standoff.

source.title: Spokane Transit Authority considers changes to bus routes in 2026
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: STA proposes ending bus service through the Peaceful Valley neighborhood, citing low ridership, to redirect resources toward requested service in Hillyard.

source.title: 2026 Service Revisions – Final Report
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: STA's own final report on the 2026 changes, including public comments objecting to reduced service in neighborhoods such as Peaceful Valley and Vinegar Flats/Latah Valley.

source.title: Spokane business group denies public access as it lobbies transit agency
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: Reports that Greater Spokane Inc. organized a closed-door meeting to lobby STA against a permanent tax renewal; a Spokane Valley council member and STA board member urged the board to delay its vote to accommodate the business group.

source.title: Spokane Transit Authority waffles on tax renewal vote amid whispers of opposition campaign
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: STA's board debates delaying its ballot measure amid pressure tied to a competing county public-safety tax proposal also being prepared for the ballot.

source.title: Voters narrowly approving Spokane Transit Authority's 20-year tax renewal on Tuesday
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: Reports the measure passing with roughly 50.4% support; opponents had argued STA's more than $250 million in reserves meant the renewal was unnecessary.

source.title: Truth tester: How do claims stack up on Spokane Transit Authority tax renewal advertisements?
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: Fact-checks campaign advertising from both sides ahead of the vote; notes opponents raised and spent roughly two-thirds of the nearly $250,000 in total campaign spending.

source.title: Tax supporters file complaint alleging opposition group misleading voters on STA renewal
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: A state Public Disclosure Commission complaint accuses an opposition group of misleading voters about whether service cuts would follow a failed renewal.

source.title: Spokane Transit seeks to renew sales tax; opponents say the timing is wrong
source.section: Spokane Transit Authority
source.description: Business-aligned critics argue transit funding shouldn't be prioritized given other crises like overdose deaths; STA says a rejected renewal would cost about $30 million a year starting in 2029.

source.title: Spokane Public Library seeks funding increase to avoid program and resource cuts
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: Library officials warn of reduced hours, fewer programs, and diminished collections after a 5% cut to the system's city funding in 2025.

source.title: Library Board of Trustees: The Spokane Public Library is essential to our community
source.outlet: The Spokesman-Review (guest opinion, Library Board of Trustees)
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: The library board's public appeal for restored funding, stating the system has “reached a breaking point” and can no longer keep branches open seven days a week without it.

source.title: Spokane library director asks public to protest proposed budget cuts
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: Interview with library director Andrew Chanse on the city's proposal to extend the prior year's funding cut into 2026.

source.title: As budget deadline looms, Spokane council weighs its own budget against the library's
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: Mayor Lisa Brown's proposed budget initially kept library cuts in place, citing citywide financial pressure, before a council amendment restored partial funding.

source.title: Spokane City Council Votes on Modification For 2026 City Budget
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: Announces the council's 5–2 vote restoring library, City Cable 5, and public defender funding while emphasizing minimal staff cuts elsewhere.

source.title: Spokane library warns service cuts could start by September
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: Reports the library's reserves are now depleted after absorbing earlier shortfalls, and that roughly $2.3 million in city funding is needed to avoid new cuts.

source.title: Spokane library deficit could force cuts to staff, services, branch availability
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: Outlines specific cut scenarios under consideration: closing every branch on Sundays and one on Mondays, laying off 3.5 full-time staff, and cutting senior- and daycare-center services by 10%.

source.title: Spokane council backs budget priorities ahead of another potential shortfall
source.section: City of Spokane — Library & Civic Budget Cuts
source.description: Notes the city and county both anticipate 2027 deficits, with transit, school, and public-safety tax measures all competing for the same voters in the same election cycle.

source.title: Spokane Valley passes ‘not a sanctuary city’ resolution meant to show allegiance to Trump
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: The council votes 5–2 to reaffirm opposition to the state's sanctuary law; the sponsoring councilwoman says the goal was to “send a message to President Donald Trump.”

source.title: Spokane Valley City Council votes to pass non-sanctuary resolution
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Overview of the resolution, which updates a 2016 predecessor to align with Washington's 2019 Keep Washington Working Act.

source.title: NEWS BRIEFS: Spokane Valley affirms it's not a sanctuary city
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Notes the same 5–2 vote alongside Spokane's contemporaneous, and very different, debate over a proposed “Homeless Bill of Rights.”

source.title: ‘Not a sanctuary city’: Spokane Valley resolution ignites immigration debate
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Ties the vote to U.S. Rep. Michael Baumgartner's parallel effort in Congress requesting information on the state's sanctuary law, and quotes the county sheriff's office saying its practices won't change either way.

source.title: Spokane Valley City Council passes resolution declaring it is not a ‘Sanctuary City’
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: A local immigrant-advocacy nonprofit argues sanctuary policies improve public safety; two councilmembers, Ben Wick and Tim Hattenburg (per later coverage), cast the dissenting votes.

source.title: Spokane Valley City Council votes unanimously to further criminalize homelessness
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Council adopts a citywide camping ban shortly after the U.S. Supreme Court's Grants Pass ruling; one member's push to require homeless individuals to prove citizenship was not adopted in this ordinance.

source.title: Spokane County leaders enact new code on private camping to combat nuisance properties
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: County commissioners cite Spokane Valley's 2024 ordinance (up to 90 days in jail for camping in a park after hours) as a model for their own new private-property camping code.

source.title: Spokane Valley Debates Limiting Flags on Public Property
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Council debates a policy restricting which flags may fly on city property, citing the Supreme Court's Shurtleff v. City of Boston decision; two councilmembers argue the draft policy is too vague.

source.title: Councilmembers Elect New Mayor and Deputy Mayor
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: The council selects Laura Padden as Mayor (council chair) and Tim Hattenburg — the council's only member with Democratic Party ties — as Deputy Mayor for 2026–2027.

source.title: Democrat seeks second term on Spokane Valley City Council, faces off against conservative challenger Rob Chase
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Profiles Hattenburg as the only elected Spokane Valley official without Republican Party ties, running against a former GOP state legislator who has advocated splitting eastern Washington into its own state.

source.title: Spokane Valley councilman Al Merkel to lead county GOP resolutions committee following public records controversy
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Confirms the council's Republican alignment and quotes a colleague's comment that “Republicans are the party of faith, family and freedom, but freedom comes with obeying laws.”

source.title: Judge Rules Against Councilmember Al Merkel
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: A Spokane County Superior Court judge finds Councilmember Merkel violated the council's social-media policy and the state Public Records Act, following the council's 6–0 vote to sue one of its own members.

source.title: Spokane Valley City Council will sue Councilman Al Merkel over Public Records Act fight
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Details the council's unanimous vote to sue Merkel and his threatened countersuit alleging civil-rights violations.

source.title: WATCH: Spokane Valley meeting ends abruptly after exchange over councilmember lawsuit
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Mayor Padden cuts Merkel's microphone as the city tallies roughly $600,000 in taxpayer costs tied to the internal dispute; a colleague calls Merkel “a spoiled child” on the dais.

source.title: Spokane Valley City Council pulls public safety funding to cover costs of struggles with Councilman Al Merkel
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Council reallocates funds earmarked for public safety to help cover legal costs from the internal Merkel dispute.

source.title: Spokane Valley spat may erode public records rules
source.section: Spokane Valley City Council
source.description: Examines how the Merkel fight is shaping a statewide legislative debate over public-records exemptions, with transparency advocates warning against “incremental whittling away” of open-government law.

source.title: Sheriffs including Spokane County's John Nowels sues to block new standards for county sheriff
source.section: Spokane County Government
source.description: Nowels joins three other Eastern Washington sheriffs suing the state over a new law adding qualification standards and a state commission's oversight authority for elected sheriffs.

source.title: Spokane County Commission to consider public safety sales tax that wouldn't need voter approval
source.section: Spokane County Government
source.description: County commissioners weigh a state law allowing a public-safety sales tax without a public vote, amid a broader county budget shortfall.

source.title: Spokane County weighs sales tax process to avoid sheriff cuts
source.section: Spokane County Government
source.description: Sheriff Nowels warns that without new revenue, “significant services being canceled” is likely, following an earlier voter rejection of a separate jail-focused public-safety tax.

source.title: Spokane Valley taxpayers face higher costs if city doesn't renew policing contract
source.section: Spokane County Government
source.description: Sheriff Nowels and county officials detail the rising cost (up 70% in five years) of the contract that supplies Spokane Valley's police services through the Sheriff's Office.

source.title: With progressive council wins, Spokane swings left

source.title: Spokane progressives could clinch complete seven-member council majority next fall
source.section: Spokane vs. Spokane Valley Divide
source.description: Covers the swearing-in of new progressive council members and the shrinking two-member conservative minority, one of whom has said he plans not to seek re-election.

source.title: ‘God help us’: Conservatives feel iced out by new, more progressive Spokane City Council
source.section: Spokane vs. Spokane Valley Divide
source.description: The council's remaining conservative members describe losing influence over committee assignments and procedural leadership roles as the council's ideological composition shifted further left.

source.title: Spokane favor incumbents as conservatives fall short on bid to expand minority
source.section: Spokane vs. Spokane Valley Divide
source.description: Recaps 2025 election results across the Spokane City Council, Spokane Municipal Court, and Spokane Valley races.

source.title: Seattle nonprofit will bus advocates to Spokane to campaign for local progressives
source.section: Spokane vs. Spokane Valley Divide
source.description: Describes a Seattle-based group canvassing for Spokane's progressive council candidates, and a local conservative PAC's counter-spending for their opponents.

source.title: Spokane council sets aside ideological divide to replace unenforceable camping ban
source.section: Spokane vs. Spokane Valley Divide
source.description: A unanimous, election-week reversal of the mayor's camping policy; a resident testifies it is “a shell game” timed to protect council seats before the election.

source.title: Spokane conservatives to reintroduce voters' camping ban
source.section: Spokane vs. Spokane Valley Divide
source.description: Covers conservative councilmembers Jonathan Bingle and Michael Cathcart's repeated, twice-rejected push to restore the voter-approved Prop 1 camping ban.

source.title: Spokane progressives surrender on homeless camping ban, adopt conservative enforcement plan before election
source.section: Spokane vs. Spokane Valley Divide
source.description: An outlet critical of the reversal frames the council's unanimous vote as capitulating to conservative pressure and business-community backlash ahead of the election.

source.title: WA Supreme Court strikes down camping ban backed by 75% of Spokane voters

source.description: Background on the original voter-approved Prop 1 camping ban and the state Supreme Court ruling that set off a year of fights over its replacement.

source.title: Idaho is the Epicenter American Redoubt Movement
source.outlet: Kootenai Democrats (Idaho county Democratic Party organization)
source.section: American Redoubt and the Broader Christian-Nationalist Migration Movement
source.description: A regional Democratic Party organization's response to the same reporting, describing an ongoing effort by Redoubt-aligned figures to “assume control” of local governments in the Inland Northwest.

source.title: The Hop! is closing but moving
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Owner T.C. Chavez closes the original Hop! all-ages venue at 706 N. Monroe — which had survived a fatal 2013 parking-lot shooting — after the building's owner put it up for sale, and shifts his focus to a new downtown club, Pinnacle Northwest (“the Pin”), at 412 W. Sprague.

source.title: Vinther and Nelson Hardware Building (706 N. Monroe St.) — Spokane Register of Historic Places Nomination
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: The city's own nomination document for the building that later housed the Hop notes it “has now remained vacant for several years,” the latest chapter in a building that has cycled between occupied and vacant repeatedly since the 1960s.

source.title: Spokane music venue the Pin announces closure
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Pinnacle Northwest (“the Pin”), the downtown all-ages club that had hosted acts from the Misfits' Michale Graves to touring country and rap performers, announces its permanent closure; owner Chelsey Heidenreich cites pandemic-era uncertainty over when the venue could reopen.

source.title: Spokane music venue 'The Pin' announces permanent closure
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Confirms the same closure and reprints the owners' Facebook statement thanking staff and patrons for “the best time.”

source.title: ‘It's time’: After 44 years, iconic Spokane event Pig Out in the Park comes to an end
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Founder Bill Burke ends Riverfront Park's long-running free food-and-music festival after 44 years, citing his own age (“I am going to be 75 this year”) rather than a single external cause. Included as a notable loss of a long-running cultural event rather than a business.

source.title: Restaurant closures pile up in Spokane area
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: At least seven Spokane restaurants close within about two months, including Suki Yaki Inn (open since 1949) and the Red Lion Pub (since 1960); a hospitality-industry trade group president cites higher minimum wages, food costs, and lingering COVID-era debt, while noting Spokane sales growth has not kept pace with inflation.

source.title: Red Lion Pub, Suki Yaki among restaurants closing in downtown Spokane
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Spokane's paper of record covers the same closure wave among downtown restaurants heading into the new year.

source.title: Experts weigh in on why several Spokane restaurants are closing their doors
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Names Crave Eats. Drinks. Nightlife, the Red Lion Pub, Suki Yaki, and BRGR House among the closures and examines contributing economic factors with industry sources.

source.title: Industry experts weigh in on Spokane's rash of restaurant closures
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Additional coverage of the same closure wave, noting the data on the year's full closure count was still incomplete at publication.

source.title: Employees dazed and confused after Shenanigans' abrupt closure
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: C.I. Shenanigans, a downtown fixture for more than 30 years, closes abruptly on a Saturday night, leaving about 40 employees suddenly out of work.

source.title: North Spokane's B&B Hobbies to close after 60 years in business
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: The Batch brothers close the hobby shop their parents opened in 1965, describing loyal customers spanning four and five generations even as the closure proceeds.

source.title: Spokane-area bike shop peddles off into the sunset
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: The Bike Hub, open since 2009, closes its last remaining location in Spokane Valley; its downtown and South Hill locations had each already closed in the preceding two years.

source.title: Downtown Spokane salon closes doors, citing Catholic Charities housing and crime
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: The co-owner of Urbanna Natural Spa, Salon and Wine says crime associated with nearby Catholic Charities low-income housing drove her to close permanently; the city cites SPD data showing about 6,200 arrests in the surrounding corridor in 2024–25, with 24 individuals responsible for over a third of that activity, and describes recent enforcement changes in the area.

source.title: Art studio moving out of downtown Spokane
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Pinot's Palette, a paint-and-sip art studio, leaves its downtown space for a larger East Sprague location with its own parking lot. A relocation rather than a closure, included here as another downtown departure.

source.title: Spokane business leader says downtown's vacancy rate is up to 28%: 'That's a little scary'
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: A commercial real-estate executive tells a university audience downtown's commercial vacancy rate has reached 28%, and says perceptions of crime and visible homelessness complicate efforts to attract tenants.

source.title: High office vacancy challenges downtown core
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Central Business District office vacancy climbs to 31% in fall 2025, the highest in roughly three decades, attributed to post-pandemic remote work, aging buildings, rising rents, and safety concerns; notes insurer Travelers vacated 75,000 square feet downtown in 2024 and moved to a smaller Spokane Valley office.

source.title: Inland Northwest Business Watch: The Clock Is Ticking on Spokane's Commercial Core
source.outlet: Inland Northwest Business Watch (independent local business blog)
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: An independent local business blog argues roughly 2,000 fewer downtown workers a day since 2023 represents a structural shift rather than a temporary dip, compounding a national wave of more than 8,200 retail closures in 2025.

source.title: Downtown Spokane block closed for 14 months for ambitious development causing consternation for businesses
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: A 13-year-old bar's owner describes his worst single day of business as construction fencing for the Peyton Building's $33 million apartment conversion cuts off Post Street foot traffic for over a year.

source.title: The 12 big questions facing Spokane and Washington state leaders in 2026
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: Names high downtown vacancy, falling property values, and public unease about safety among the year's central civic challenges, alongside the city's 20-year comprehensive plan process and a possible renewed county public-safety tax measure.

source.title: Downtown Spokane sees new business growth amid ongoing vacancy challenges
source.section: Business, Music-Venue, and Downtown Closures
source.description: The Downtown Spokane Partnership reports 27 new ground-floor businesses opened in 2025, more than in 2024, even as the group says empty storefronts remain a challenge. Included for the fuller context behind the closures listed above.

source.title: Spokane fires destroy hundreds of structures
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: About 700 structures were destroyed and more than 65,000 people were under evacuation orders as of Sunday morning; Mayor Lisa Brown called it “the worst natural disaster our region has faced,” and Gov. Bob Ferguson declared a statewide wildfire emergency and burn ban.

source.title: ‘Overwhelming amount of damage’: Fight ongoing against Spokane fires
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: The three fires had scorched more than 10,000 acres with no containment; officials announced the arson arrest connected to the Old Trails Fire the same night.

source.title: Wildfires Near Spokane Destroy More Than 700 Buildings, Force 64,000 to Flee
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: The Spokane fires ranked as the top U.S. firefighting priority amid dozens of major blazes burning across the drought-parched Pacific Northwest.

source.title: More than 700 structures lost as 65,000 evacuate in Washington state wildfires
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Names the three fires — Old Trails (3,619 acres), Fairview (1,056 acres), and Autumn Lane (3,351 acres) — and quotes Sen. Maria Cantwell describing the event as driven by “a historic weather event.”

source.title: ‘A tremendous tragedy’: thousands evacuated, hundreds of structures destroyed in Spokane Area Fires
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Final structure count reached 921 damaged or destroyed across the three fires, with nearly 2,000 fire personnel from 176 jurisdictions assisting; Gov. Ferguson said he spoke directly with President Trump about federal support.

source.title: Urban firestorm devastates Spokane as dense smoke envelops the Northwest
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Describes it as the most destructive wildfire in Washington state history, driven by sustained winds of 33 mph gusting to 44 mph, 86-degree heat, and 20–25% relative humidity.

source.title: ‘It doesn't seem real’: Spokane is a community in mourning as the toll of destruction from weekend wildfires comes into focus
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Returning residents and the state's adjutant general describe the leveled Rifle Club Road neighborhood as a “war zone.”

source.title: Man arrested on suspicion of arson for allegedly starting Spokane fire
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Aaron Farinacci, 37, was arrested and charged with first-degree arson for the Old Trails Fire; he was found about 1.5 miles from the fire's start with waterproof matches and a butane lighter.

source.title: Spokane wildfire arson suspect makes first court appearance
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Farinacci is accused of “knowingly and maliciously” causing the most destructive of the three blazes in a city of about 230,000 people.

source.title: Court docs: Spokane arson suspect told police he set 25 fires over the past year
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Farinacci told investigators he had started 25 fires over the prior year; four were corroborated and added as charges, and the court ordered a mental competency evaluation.

source.title: Man charged with setting devastating Spokane fire to be evaluated for competency to stand trial
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Farinacci now faces five counts of first-degree arson; a witness who twice passed him near a tree line shortly before the fire started helped identify him as a suspect.

source.title: Spokane wildfire arson suspect had prior manslaughter conviction; blazes leave some residents with nothing
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Reports Farinacci's prior manslaughter conviction and notes the fires occurred in the wildland-urban interface, where homes sit at the edge of wildland vegetation.

source.title: Man accused of arson in the biggest of 3 major fires in Spokane, Washington
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Farinacci was taken into custody with SWAT assistance; prosecutors say he had been questioned about “arson-related behavior” in the past without arrest, and had a 2012 Arizona manslaughter conviction tied to a 2010 killing.

source.title: Alleged arsonist admits to starting one Spokane wildfire and more than two dozen others since last year, prosecutors say
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: A nearby resident's reaction (“That S.O.B. started a fire”) is quoted alongside details of the additional charges and $2 million bond.

source.title: Arson Suspect Timed Spokane Fire for High Wind Day
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Court documents say Farinacci told a detective he planned the fire to coincide with a forecast “high winds” day.

source.title: Man charged with series of July fires sentenced to prison
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: A separate, unrelated repeat arsonist, Chad A. Horne, 38, was sentenced to 63 months after pleading guilty to three counts of second-degree arson for a string of July 2025 fires across Kendall Yards, downtown, and East Central Spokane, including the My Fresh Basket grocery store and a WSU-Spokane EV charging station; he had prior 2024 reckless-burning convictions.

source.title: Man pleads guilty to downtown Spokane arson, sentenced to over five years
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: The sentencing judge ordered Horne to undergo substance-abuse and mental-health evaluations and said she hoped he would stay on his medications.

source.title: Man sentenced to over 5 years in prison for setting string of fires in Spokane last summer
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Surveillance video showed a repeated pattern of Horne's presence at a location followed by a fire report at that same spot across several Spokane streets in a single morning.

source.title: Downtown Spokane arson suspect confesses to setting fires
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Covers Horne's July 2025 arrest and confession, his prior December 2024 guilty plea for a fire that damaged a fence and a dog-grooming business, and a separate, uncharged investigation into 11 fires along the High Drive bluff trail in which he was named a “potential suspect.”

source.title: Suspected arsonist identified after Spokane fire spree
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Details Horne's earlier June 2024 arrest for fires near a homeless shelter, including a business fire and a portable toilet burned “from the inside out,” after an acquaintance witnessed him lighting one of the fires.

source.title: Spokane area businesses warned against price gouging after fires
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: The Washington Attorney General's Office warns retailers against exploiting emergency demand for essential goods and services under the state Consumer Protection Act.

source.title: How to help: City of Spokane creates portal to organize donations for wildfire recovery
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: A Spokane County commissioner warns fire victims that people offering repair work or expensive services are “not the best actors” and often don't deliver.

source.title: Wildfires threaten to further strain Spokane area's housing market: ‘It's going to have a huge impact’
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Describes rising building-material costs, an already-tight housing inventory, and the Spokane Housing Authority's own staff — 15 of 95 employees — among those displaced.

source.title: Spokane Agents Jump Into Action As Wildfires Devastate Housing
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: A local broker says Spokane's permitting process was already slow before the fires and warns rebuilding hundreds of homes will strain contractors, materials, and permitting offices further; compares the recovery ahead to Altadena/Pacific Palisades and Lahaina.

source.title: Spokane devastation pressures Washington's burdened homeowners' insurance market
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Warns of wildfire coverage caps, restricted loss-of-use benefits, and hotel shortages that may push displaced families outside the city and disrupt schooling.

source.title: Spokane wildfires highlight insurance crisis for homeowners across US
source.section: The August 2026 Wildfires and a Pattern of Arson
source.description: Notes this is the third time since 2020 a wildland fire has become a destructive urban firestorm, after Colorado (2021) and California (2025), as insurers increasingly restrict coverage in fire-prone areas nationally.

source.title: Northern Idaho employers losing to Washington's minimum wage
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: A Post Falls hospital's HR director says housekeepers and certified nursing assistants made up over a third of the hospital's turnover as workers left for higher pay in Spokane, 17 miles away.

source.title: As Idaho's Neighboring States Increase Minimum Wage, More Workers Could Seek Jobs Out Of State
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: An Idaho Department of Labor economist says the Kootenai County–Spokane County wage gap keeps widening, with Kootenai's median wage running nearly 20% below Spokane's across all occupations.

source.title: Bottom Rung: Why One Idaho Border Business Chose Washington
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: Academic research on 316 pairs of border counties nationally found no net job losses from minimum-wage increases on average; a Greater Spokane Inc. official separately recalls specific employers, like a bakery, relocating to Idaho over wage costs.

source.title: Border Cities Affected by Minimum Wage Differences
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: Of workers commuting out of Kootenai County for jobs, well over half — 8,800 of 15,600 — work in Washington State, a larger out-of-state share than commuters from any other part of Idaho.

source.title: Idaho Minimum Wage 2026: Rates & Exemptions
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: Confirms Idaho's minimum wage remains pegged to the federal $7.25 floor and state law bars cities, including Coeur d'Alene, from setting a local minimum above it, while Washington's 2026 rate is described as more than double.

source.title: Occupational Employment and Wages in Coeur d'Alene — May 2025
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: Coeur d'Alene's average hourly wage of $28.88 trails the national average of $33.54; food-service and personal-care occupations there pay well under $20 an hour.

source.title: ‘Deals and a race to the bottom’: A glance at the weed industry on 4/20
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: The general manager of downtown Spokane's Lucky Leaf dispensary says sales dropped two-thirds in a single day when a larger competitor opened nearby; statewide cannabis revenue fell from about $1.47 billion in 2021 to roughly $1.14 billion in 2025.

source.title: Washington cannabis sales slipped to $1.14 billion in 2025
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: Cites a 21% drop from the 2021 peak and a state audit finding 20% annual attrition among cannabis producers and processors in 2022, versus 7% among retailers.

source.title: After pandemic high, WA weed industry finds itself in a funk
source.section: Cross-Border Economic Strain
source.description: A shop owner describes monthly after-tax sales falling from about $700,000 during the pandemic to $500,000 as demand cooled and household budgets tightened.

source.title: ‘The public would be shocked’: Nonprofits see teen victims, while authorities focus on sex trade
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Homeland Security Investigations says it arrests roughly 40 suspected pedophiles a year in the Spokane area; local nonprofit the Jonah Project says it has helped stabilize about 300 trafficking victims, almost all in their teens.

source.title: Sex Trafficking Operation
source.outlet: City of Spokane Police Department (press release)
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: A multi-agency operation at an Airway Heights casino connects a trafficked juvenile with her family and describes sex trafficking as “reportedly the fastest growing criminal industry in the world today.”

source.title: Sex Trafficking Suspect in Custody
source.outlet: City of Spokane Police Department (press release)
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: A months-long investigation, opened after a tip from Idaho authorities, leads to a Spokane man's arrest on trafficking, rape, and related charges involving a teenage victim.

source.title: 2 victims found in Spokane massage parlor linked to human trafficking
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: The Spokane County Sheriff's Office identifies two suspected trafficking victims during a search warrant at a North Division Street massage parlor.

source.title: Five Coeur d'Alene massage parlors lose licenses amid sex trafficking allegations
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Coeur d'Alene revokes five massage parlors' business licenses after a police investigation found evidence of illegal sexual activity and possible trafficking; prosecutors decline criminal charges, citing the difficulty of prosecution.

source.title: Coeur d'Alene police investigating allegations of criminal sexual activity at 5 massage parlors
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Names the five parlors and quotes police describing how potentially trafficked women are moved between businesses and towns once identified.

source.title: Revocation of license for business linked to 'illegal sexual activity' upheld
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: The city council upholds one revocation 4–2 after a contested hearing; the police chief says a separate, ongoing trafficking investigation by another agency is underway.

source.title: CDA City Council strengthens regulations for massage businesses to curb illicit activity
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: The council tightens licensing and background-check requirements for massage businesses in response to the trafficking allegations.

source.title: Attorney General files criminal charges against Spokane-based health business for fraud, organized crime
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Charges a Spokane home-health company and its owner with Leading Organized Crime, 20 counts of money laundering, 43 counts of Medicaid false statements, and witness tampering.

source.title: Spokane cigarette wholesalers indicted
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Historical case charging Spokane wholesale distributors with 27 counts of money laundering tied to smuggling untaxed cigarettes from smoke shops on the Coeur d'Alene Indian Reservation to a dozen Washington locations.

source.title: Thirty-Four Individuals Indicted in Eastern Washington
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: A years-long task-force investigation spanning Spokane County and other jurisdictions alleges a continuing criminal enterprise involving drug distribution, illegal firearms, and laundering the proceeds.

source.title: I-90 drug interdiction nets 6 arrests
source.section: Trafficking and Organized Crime in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Idaho State Police traffic stops on I-90 lead to methamphetamine and fentanyl trafficking arrests, including Spokane residents; state data shows rising regional drug-trafficking activity and overdose deaths.

source.title: Main Market Co-Op could close doors in 2024
source.section: Food Access
source.description: Reports on the nonprofit downtown grocery co-op's finances as pandemic-era loan support that had kept it afloat ran out.

source.title: Downtown Spokane's Main Market is at risk of closing, increasing food insecurity in the city's lowest income ZIP code
source.section: Food Access
source.description: Without renewed community support, Main Market — the only full grocery serving downtown's 99201 ZIP code, where about half of residents live below the federal poverty line — warned it might close by year's end. The co-op remained open as of August 2026, per its current posted hours and listings.

source.title: KNCA Dissolution Announcement
source.section: Convention and Festival Cancellations
source.description: The nonprofit behind KuroNekoCon, Spokane's anime convention running since 2011, announces it is dissolving. It says 2024 attendance (1,060) funded that event but fell short of the 1,500–2,000 needed to afford the same venue in 2025, and that efforts to find an alternative venue or funding were unsuccessful.

source.title: Police in Idaho arrested dozens of Patriot Front members near a Pride event
source.section: Extremism in Coeur d'Alene
source.description: Thirty-one suspected Patriot Front members were arrested after a tip that they were loading into a U-Haul with masks and shields; the piece notes armed “patriot” groups had drawn criticism in Coeur d'Alene two years earlier during 2020 protests, and that several self-described Christian nationalists hold local elected office in the area.

source.title: Police in Idaho are getting death threats after arresting Patriot Front members
source.section: Extremism in Coeur d'Alene
source.description: Coeur d'Alene's police chief reports his department received death threats after the arrests; the piece also describes a Christian-nationalist activist leading a prayer protest against the same Pride event at the public library.

source.title: Suspected members of the neo-Nazi Patriot Front arrested at Pride event
source.section: Extremism in Coeur d'Alene
source.description: Additional detail on the arrests and the group's 2017 formation out of Vanguard America following the “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia.

source.title: White nationalists convicted of planning to riot at Idaho pride event
source.section: Extremism in Coeur d'Alene
source.description: A Kootenai County jury convicts five of the 31 arrested men of misdemeanor conspiracy to riot after about an hour of deliberation.

source.title: Patriot Front members to serve just three days in jail for plan to storm Pride event
source.section: Extremism in Coeur d'Alene
source.description: The five convicted men are sentenced to five days in jail (with credit for two days served), a $1,000 fine, a year of unsupervised probation, and a one-year bar from the park — a sentence reported as notably light relative to the alleged riot plot.

source.title: Patriot Front Members Arrested on Way to Target Pride Event
source.section: Extremism in Coeur d'Alene
source.description: Coeur d'Alene's then-mayor, Jim Hammond, says the city rejects “the days of the Aryans,” referencing Aryan Nations founder Richard Butler's 1999 parade through downtown; notes all 31 arrested were from outside the local area.

source.title: 2017 Freeman High School shooting
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: A 15-year-old student opened fire in a hallway at Freeman High School in Rockford, Washington, on Sept. 13, 2017, killing one classmate and injuring three others before a school custodian intervened and disarmed him.

source.title: Judge: Teen charged in Freeman High School shooting to be tried as adult
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: A Spokane County judge rules Caleb Sharpe, who was 15 at the time of the shooting, will be tried as an adult, saying “nothing about this was spontaneous.”

source.title: ‘I thought I was going to die’: Girl shot at Freeman High School gives impact statement
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: Coverage of Sharpe's guilty plea hearing, at which surviving victim Jordyn Goldsmith and the parents of Sam Strahan, the 15-year-old killed while confronting the shooter, gave victim-impact statements.

source.title: Washington school shooter sentenced to 40 years in prison for 2017 rampage at Freeman High School
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: Sharpe is sentenced to 40 years after pleading guilty to premeditated murder, three counts of attempted murder, and second-degree assault; the sentencing judge showed surveillance footage of the attack in court.

source.title: Freeman High School shooter resentenced to 25 years to life behind bars
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: A state appeals court finds Sharpe's original 40-year sentence unconstitutional under a law capping sentences at 25 years to life for crimes committed before age 16; he is resentenced accordingly.

source.title: Suspect in Shooting that Took the Life of a 13-year-old Identified
source.outlet: City of Spokane Police Department (press release)
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: Names Glen Dylan Burkey, 25, as the suspect in the Jan. 25 drive-by shooting death of 13-year-old Gavin Looper in the Hillyard neighborhood, warning the public he should be considered armed and dangerous.

source.title: Man suspected of killing 13-year-old in Hillyard waives extradition after arrest in Missoula
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: Court documents say Burkey fired five times into the back door of a home where Looper, playing video games in a bedroom, was struck in the head; a Washington SWAT standoff near Burkey's home preceded a multi-day manhunt that ended with his arrest in Missoula, Montana.

source.title: Man suspected of killing 13-year-old to be extradited to Washington state
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: Burkey is located in Missoula after a brief SWAT standoff in which officers used flash-bangs to bring him out of a home; he waives extradition and is returned to Spokane County on $3 million bond.

source.title: Mother of 13-year-old killed in North Spokane shooting speaks at suspect's bond hearing
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: Looper's mother, Renee Rogers, asks the court to keep Burkey, now charged with first-degree murder, held on $2 million bond, saying he had “made a mockery of his release conditions and probation too many times.”

source.title: Friend of accused killer of 13-year-old sentenced to prison for paying to hide him
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: Mason Bolton is sentenced to nearly four years after pleading guilty to paying to help hide Burkey in Montana; Burkey's mother, Becky Gibbs, separately faces a charge of rendering criminal assistance for helping her son flee the state. Burkey himself remained awaiting trial as of this reporting.

source.title: SPD continues search for drive-by shooter
source.outlet: City of Spokane Police Department (press release)
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: One of several summer 2024 drive-by incidents; a man is shot outside a gas station on North Monroe Street and hospitalized with serious injuries.

source.title: Police Department News Releases for 2024 (July 22–25 cluster)
source.outlet: City of Spokane Police Department (press release archive)
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: SPD's own release log shows two separate drive-by shooting calls within a half hour of each other on the evening of July 24, another shooting the following morning, and a homicide investigation the same week — illustrating how such incidents can cluster.

source.title: Male In Custody After North Spokane Drive By Shooting
source.outlet: City of Spokane Police Department (press release)
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: A man fires a handgun from a pickup truck and displays a firearm at multiple west Spokane locations before leading officers on a pursuit that ends when he crashes into a patrol vehicle.

source.title: Police investigate possible drive-by shooting in Spokane's West Central neighborhood
source.section: Major Violence
source.description: About 15 patrol cars pursue a suspect fleeing a shooting scene near Spokane Falls Community College before he is detained east of Audubon Park.

source.title: Protesters rally at Spokane ICE after detainment of asylum seeker
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Stuckart, on Facebook, calls for support after ICE detains Cesar Alexander Alvarez Perez, a 21-year-old Venezuelan asylum seeker in Stuckart's care as a legal guardian, along with a Colombian friend, during what was billed as a routine check-in.

source.title: More than 30 arrested at immigration protest in Spokane sparked by arrest of 2 immigrants
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Police Chief Kevin Hall says about 185 city officers responded as demonstrators blocked ICE vehicles; officers used smoke grenades and pepper balls (not rubber bullets, Hall said) after acknowledging some in the crowd were committing crimes.

source.title: Everything we know about the Spokane ICE protests
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: A running explainer noting Stuckart was denied entry to the ICE check-in and only learned of the detention afterward, and compiling statements and coverage from other local outlets as the story developed.

source.title: Stuckart released from jail as Spokane Police Department requests felony charges after arrest at immigration protest
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Stuckart says he formed a human chain around the ICE bus for roughly six hours before his arrest; Mayor Lisa Brown had declared a 9:30 p.m. curfew after the protest grew to about 1,000 people.

source.title: Former Spokane councilman arrested at ICE protest released from Spokane County jail
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Stuckart was held on a $500 bond for failure to disperse; more than 30 people were arrested total as the protest escalated.

source.title: Pepper-balls vs. tear gas: How 2020's Black Lives Matter protest in Spokane compares to the immigration demonstration of 2025
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Notes it was the first Spokane mayoral curfew since the May 2020 George Floyd protests, and compares the scale and police response of both events directly.

source.title: Federal government accuses nine Spokane protesters of violence against ICE
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: A federal grand jury indicts Stuckart and eight others on charges of using “force and threats” to impede federal agents; U.S. Sen. Patty Murray and Mayor Brown instead blame the federal government's own tactics.

source.title: KIRO hosts raise alarm over ICE tactics after 9 arrested in Spokane
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Discusses the indictment and quotes Stuckart describing the two young men he was advocating for as legal immigrants who “did exactly what they were told” before being detained anyway.

source.title: Former Spokane City Council president pleads guilty to impeding ICE officers to prevent the deportation of two legal immigrants
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Stuckart pleads guilty to a felony charge of impeding immigration officers; the two men he tried to protect, both in the U.S. through a humanitarian parole program the Trump administration did not extend, worked steady jobs and attended church locally.

source.title: Former Spokane official pleads guilty after ICE blockade
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Outside the courthouse, Stuckart said he “accepted full responsibility” and felt he “had to take a stand”; the felony carries a possible sentence of up to six years, though a later plea change was under consideration.

source.title: Northwest lawmakers weigh in on ICE conduct as impasse leads to Homeland Security shutdown
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Rep. Michael Baumgartner says better local-federal cooperation could “bring down the temperature,” as Northwest lawmakers split along party lines over ICE conduct.

source.title: News Roundup: Immigration, TPS and ICE in Spokane
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Reports Rep. Baumgartner expressed sympathy over deaths linked to federal immigration operations while defending ICE's role enforcing laws passed by Congress; Rep. Dan Newhouse, R-Sunnyside, said enforcement had “gotten out of hand.”

source.title: Spokane County Republican Party endorses Donald Trump, Semi Bird
source.section: Trump Allegiance
source.description: The county party's full 2024 endorsement slate includes Trump for president and gubernatorial candidate Semi Bird, who separately drew controversy over allegedly misrepresenting his military record and a past misdemeanor.

source.title: The Washington GOP convention kicks off Thursday in Spokane. Here's what's at stake
source.section: Trump Allegiance
source.description: Trump's Truth Social endorsement of primary challenger Jerrod Sessler over incumbent Rep. Dan Newhouse (“Jerrod Sessler is MAGA all the way... He will never let you down!!!”) becomes a central issue as the state party gathers in Spokane to consider early endorsements.

source.title: Washington Republicans get ready to rumble in Spokane
source.section: Trump Allegiance
source.description: Notes that all 10 House Republicans who voted to impeach Trump in 2021, including two Washington members, faced intense delegate scrutiny at the Spokane convention; Baumgartner, then Spokane County treasurer, is described as the fundraising leader in the open 5th District race.

source.title: WA GOP wraps up turbulent state convention in Spokane
source.section: Trump Allegiance
source.description: Candidates were asked to sign a pledge to end their campaigns and unite behind the delegate-endorsed nominee; a former state lawmaker who withdrew after signing said he was “hoping the delegates would have a longer view... versus a purity test.”

source.title: Baumgartner Issues Statement on Protests in Spokane Last Night
source.section: Trump Allegiance
source.description: Baumgartner calls on “local government officials in Washington state” to “work collaboratively with federal officials to enforce immigration laws,” aligning with the Trump administration's enforcement posture during the ICE protests described in Section XIX.

source.title: Endorsements by Spokane County, Wash., Republican Party
source.section: Trump Allegiance
source.description: A running, sourced list of the county party's endorsements in federal, state, and local races.

source.title: Thousands march in Spokane on Sunday to protest George Floyd's death, police brutality
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: Thousands march through downtown; law enforcement officers, including then-Police Chief Craig Meidl, are photographed kneeling with protesters at the Spokane County Courthouse earlier in the day.

source.title: Spokane police use tear gas, rubber bullets to disperse crowds downtown
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: After looting broke out at the downtown Nike store, Mayor Woodward issued an overnight curfew and Sheriff Ozzie Knezovich requested 200 Washington National Guard troops; a Lenco BearCat armored vehicle was used to help push protesters back.

source.title: Video captures looting of downtown Spokane's Nike store
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: A Spokesman-Review photographer's video shows the Nike store looting that touched off the evening's broader clashes between police and crowds.

source.title: Spokane sheriff, police chief blame Sunday's violence on outside agitators
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: Law enforcement and Spokane NAACP president Kurtis Robinson say the day's peaceful protests were “hijacked” by outside agitators, while police acknowledge downplaying the presence of armed far-right militia members who had also been in the downtown core.

source.title: Police took a behind-the-scenes approach on Sunday, and Spokane didn't experience another riot
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: A week after the riot, a similarly sized crowd marched peacefully; a police spokesman said protesters had thrown spent tear-gas canisters and improvised rock-salt explosives at officers the prior week.

source.title: Thousands of protesters gather in downtown Spokane for Sunday demonstrations against police brutality
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: A second Sunday of large, largely peaceful marches calls for police reforms “up to and including defunding the department,” while several armed men appeared downtown as the sun set.

source.title: BLM peaceful protest concludes early in downtown Spokane due to inclement weather; Separate demonstrations ensue
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: After the main rally ended, reporters observed armed counter-demonstrators in the crowd and witnessed an attempt to burn an American flag near the Riverfront Park fountain, which a bystander stopped.

source.title: Black Lives Matter mural defaced with red, white and blue paint
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: Vandals splash paint over the word “Black” in a downtown mural painted weeks earlier; the community raises over $3,000 to repair it within an hour of the damage being noticed.

source.title: Black Lives Matter protests to continue Sunday in downtown Spokane
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: A later protest responds to the Kenosha police shooting of Jacob Blake and references local backlash over the Spokane County Sheriff's Office hosting a “killology” use-of-force trainer and data showing disproportionate arrest rates for minorities.

source.title: Protesters decrying police brutality meet downtown Spokane for third straight weekend
source.section: Spokane's Response to the 2020 Black Lives Matter Protests
source.description: Spokane NAACP chapter president Kurtis Robinson leads a moment of silence as a smaller, peaceful crowd gathers for a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations.

source.title: In Washington politics, is it really Seattle's state now?
source.section: Anti-Seattle and Anti-Olympia Rhetoric in Eastern Washington
source.description: Then-House Speaker Laurie Jinkins, D-Tacoma, is quoted saying “everybody loves to hate Seattle”; the piece argues anti-Seattle sentiment in the Legislature, “especially virulent among Republicans,” has for years been used to block popular progressive policy statewide.

source.title: Shawn Vestal: Greater Idaho is a wonderful name for a bad idea
source.section: Anti-Seattle and Anti-Olympia Rhetoric in Eastern Washington
source.description: Ties Oregon's Greater Idaho push to Matt Shea's Liberty State project to split Eastern Washington into a 51st state “to omit liberals, elevate gun rights to a religion, and return to the good old days.”

source.title: Greater Idaho and the ugly history of Northwest secession movements
source.section: Anti-Seattle and Anti-Olympia Rhetoric in Eastern Washington
source.description: Traces the region's secessionist impulses to an 1865 Walla Walla Statesman editorial complaining Eastern Washington's “franchises... are not at our own disposal, but the people of the Clam country give them to whom they wish.”

source.title: Could Greater Idaho happen?
source.section: Anti-Seattle and Anti-Olympia Rhetoric in Eastern Washington
source.description: Reports that two Spokane Valley state representatives introduced Matt Shea's Liberty State bill, whose western border would run along the Cascade crest, and notes its ties to Shea's Malheur refuge and “biblical warfare” controversies.

source.title: Oregon's Greater Idaho movement echoes a long history of racism in the region
source.section: Anti-Seattle and Anti-Olympia Rhetoric in Eastern Washington
source.description: A Western States Center program director says the secession movement's rhetoric — including material published on anti-immigrant sites — amounts to a “far-right culture war” front, even though most who dismiss the idea as far-fetched are not “connecting the dots.”

source.title: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Background reference noting that as a state legislator she co-sponsored 1997 legislation banning same-sex marriage in Washington, and in 2001 blocked a bill replacing “Oriental” with “Asian” in state documents.

source.title: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Catalogs her House votes against LGBTQ-inclusive hate-crimes legislation, against employment-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people, against repealing “don't ask, don't tell,” and for a constitutional amendment defining marriage as one man and one woman.

source.title: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Notes the House Ethics Committee sanctioned her on Dec. 19, 2019, after finding she had “likely accepted official services” in violation of campaign-finance rules.

source.title: Report on Representative Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: The committee's own released report on the campaign-finance allegations against her.

source.title: Shawn Vestal: McMorris Rodgers' offensive campaign ads and flyers undermine her call for political civility
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Criticizes 2018 re-election mailers depicting a hooded man near a girl in a park, tied to a decades-old vote, as suggesting opponent Lisa Brown was soft on sexual predators; other outlets cited include the Seattle Post-Intelligencer and the Inlander.

source.title: Shawn Vestal: At long last, a great race in the 5th District
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Recaps the 2018 race, in which McMorris Rodgers later told the Inlander she regretted the tone of the ad described above, and won by 10 points.

source.title: Shawn Vestal: With her vote today, McMorris Rodgers finalizes the sale of her soul
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: A harshly critical column following her vote to object to certifying President Biden's 2020 win, quoting her saying she wanted to “give voice to the millions of Americans that do not have trust and confidence in this election.”

source.title: Vestal's hateful attack
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: A reader's published letter calls the above column a “hate-filled harangue” and defends McMorris Rodgers as “a decent, honest, duly elected representative”; included to show the published range of local reaction.

source.title: For weeks, Rep. McMorris Rodgers has refused to talk to reporters — yet invited the Spokesman-Review editor to Biden's inauguration
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Details her limited press availability in the weeks after the Jan. 6, 2021 vote, contrasted with a personal invitation extended to the Spokesman-Review's editor-in-chief.

source.title: Baumgartner faces angry, disruptive town hall following two months of Trump's presidency
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: A crowd at Whitworth University repeatedly interrupts Baumgartner during a town hall, demanding answers about his voting record and recent Trump administration actions, including his response to a refugee's question.

source.title: Rep. Baumgartner praises police for response to Spokane protest, urges cooperation with federal agents
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Baumgartner calls on Washington leaders to cooperate with ICE while Mayor Brown separately reaffirms Spokane's commitment to the state's Keep Washington Working Act, which limits local police involvement in federal immigration enforcement.

source.title: News Roundup: Immigration, TPS and ICE in Spokane
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Baumgartner responds to constituent concerns about ICE by expressing sympathy for recent deaths linked to federal operations while defending the agency's role enforcing laws passed by Congress and calling for congressional oversight hearings.

source.title: Michael Baumgartner seeks another two years in Congress
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Notes Baumgartner faces more 2026 primary challengers than in his open-seat race two years earlier, “a possible signal” some in the district see his position as more vulnerable given his association with an unpopular president, per the piece's framing.

source.title: Michael Baumgartner (Washington)
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Background reference on his prior service as a state senator (2011–2019) and Spokane County treasurer (2019–2025) before his 2024 election to Congress.

source.title: More from the Matt Shea files: GPS trackers, a ‘provisional government’ and a hunt for moles
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Follow-up on leaked emails and documents showing Shea sought to buy GPS trackers, discussed a post-collapse “provisional government,” and circulated a list of every law-enforcement officer's name and phone number in the state.

source.title: Spokane City Council members, other leaders reportedly targeted by Rep. Matt Shea call for his resignation
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Council President Ben Stuckart and colleagues Breean Beggs and Lori Kinnear call for Shea's resignation after reports he surveilled them; then-mayoral candidate Nadine Woodward issues a statement criticizing Shea's rhetoric without calling for resignation.

source.title: Spokane Police Guild joins calls for Rep. Matt Shea’s resignation over gathering of ‘intelligence’ on City Council members
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: The Spokane Police Guild adds its voice to resignation calls, saying Shea's surveillance of city officials was “appalling” and inconsistent with his duty as an elected official to uphold the Constitution.

source.title: Spokane Mayor David Condon, police Chief Craig Meidl say state Rep. Matt Shea is unfit for office
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Spokane's mayor and police chief formally declare Shea unfit for office following the surveillance revelations, joining a growing list of local officials calling for his removal from the Legislature.

source.title: Spying claims spur calls for Washington lawmaker ouster
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Wire coverage notes Spokane County Sheriff Ozzie Knezovich, a Republican, turned Shea-related documents over to the FBI and said Shea's activities were too radical for the party, while The Guardian separately reported Shea discussed “hoisting communists up flag poles” in encrypted chats.

source.title: Growing calls for Rep. Shea’s resignation, amid claims of surveillance, blacklist
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Recaps the leaked documents showing Shea compiled dossiers on progressive leaders, kept a blacklist of suspected informants, and discussed plans for a “provisional government” in case of societal collapse.

source.title: Spokane County Human Rights Task Force ‘expresses deep concern and strong denouncement of’ Matt Shea
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: The Spokane County Human Rights Task Force formally denounces Shea after the Rampart Group's domestic-terrorism report, while Spokane Valley Mayor Rod Higgins publicly voices support for Shea in the same news cycle.

source.title: Beyond DC – Mapping Stop the Steal Insurrection Rallies in the States
source.outlet: Institute for Research and Education on Human Rights (IREHR)
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: A civil-rights research group's nationwide tally of Jan. 6-adjacent “Stop the Steal” rallies lists Shea as a speaker at a Spokane rally reportedly attended by dozens, part of a wave of state-level events the day of the Capitol riot.

source.title: Matt Shea
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Background reference summarizing Shea's military service, Gonzaga law degree, House tenure from 2009-2021, and subsequent founding of On Fire Ministries & Kingdom Christian Academy after a 2021 split from Covenant Christian Church.

source.title: Redoubt movement helps push North Idaho politics to extreme right
source.section: American Redoubt and the Broader Christian-Nationalist Migration Movement
source.description: Early feature on survivalist author James Wesley Rawles's American Redoubt concept and how the influx of ideologically aligned migrants had already begun shifting North Idaho politics rightward a decade before the movement drew national attention.

source.title: How big Christian nationalism has come courting in North Idaho
source.section: American Redoubt and the Broader Christian-Nationalist Migration Movement
source.description: In-depth feature on the Redoubt's growth, fueled largely by conservative migration from California, and its political champion, Idaho state Rep. Heather Scott — described by Idaho's GOP chairman, in Marjorie Taylor Greene's presence, as “the Marjorie Taylor Greene of Idaho.” Notes Rawles's reach was amplified by Redoubt News and the Radio Free Redoubt podcast.

source.title: Extremist groups ‘popping up left and right’ in Pacific Northwest, law enforcement officials say
source.section: American Redoubt and the Broader Christian-Nationalist Migration Movement
source.description: Spokane County Sheriff Ozzie Knezovich describes monitoring threats from groups across the political spectrum in the region, including the boogaloo movement, in the wake of Proud Boys members' Jan. 6 arrests.

source.title: Ruby Ridge standoff
source.section: Aryan Nations Legacy and Ruby Ridge
source.description: Background reference on the August 1992 siege of the Weaver family's cabin near Naples, Idaho, which killed a deputy U.S. marshal, 14-year-old Samuel Weaver, and Vicki Weaver, and became a foundational grievance for the modern militia movement.

source.title: Ruby Ridge, looking back 30 years
source.section: Aryan Nations Legacy and Ruby Ridge
source.description: Thirtieth-anniversary retrospective on the 11-day standoff, noting the Weaver family had spent time at the nearby Aryan Nations compound before the siege that helped spark the growth of anti-government extremism nationally.
