source.title: Ruby Ridge siege, 25 years later, a ‘rallying cry’ for today’s white nationalists
source.section: Aryan Nations Legacy and Ruby Ridge
source.description: Published days after the Charlottesville “Unite the Right” rally, the piece traces a direct ideological line from Ruby Ridge to contemporary white-nationalist organizing, noting the Weavers' prior ties to the Aryan Nations compound.

source.title: Randy Weaver, participant in Ruby Ridge standoff, dies at 74
source.section: Aryan Nations Legacy and Ruby Ridge
source.description: Obituary noting Southern Poverty Law Center commentary that Ruby Ridge marked the opening of a new era of anti-government sentiment, and that Timothy McVeigh later cited the standoff as a motivation for the Oklahoma City bombing.

source.title: The Standoff at Ruby Ridge
source.section: Aryan Nations Legacy and Ruby Ridge
source.description: Academic public-history entry detailing how the standoff galvanized militia culture regionally and nationally, noting local Aryan Nations members were energized by the anti-government sentiment it generated.

source.title: Randy Weaver, key figure behind bloody Ruby Ridge standoff near Canada-U.S. border, dies
source.section: Aryan Nations Legacy and Ruby Ridge
source.description: Canadian public broadcaster's obituary and retrospective describing Ruby Ridge as a seminal event that mobilized militia groups nationwide and became a touchstone the movement has invoked for decades since.

source.title: The Gonzaga Center for the Study of Hate
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Institutional overview of the Gonzaga Institute for Hate Studies, founded in Spokane partly in response to Aryan Nations activity, which publishes the Journal of Hate Studies and hosts a recurring International Conference on Hate Studies.

source.title: As Hate Crimes Rise Gonzaga Convenes International Conference
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Announcement citing a 17% national rise in FBI-reported hate crimes and listing conference participants including the Kootenai County Task Force on Human Rights and the Montana Human Rights Network.

source.title: International Conference on Hate Studies 2023
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Coverage of the 2023 conference, co-hosted with the Community Colleges of Spokane, featuring keynote speaker Charlene Teters, a Spokane Tribe member and educator, addressing white supremacy and settler colonialism.

source.title: Experts: There have been warnings of far-right violence for decades, including in the Spokane area
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Gonzaga hate-studies co-founder Raymond Reyes, who has faced targeting by white supremacists during decades of work in the Inland Northwest, says the Jan. 6 Capitol riot felt familiar rather than surprising given the region's history.

source.title: As hate crimes rise nationally, so do Spokane’s community efforts to identify and eradicate them
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Reports on gaps in local hate-crime data collection between Spokane police and tribal agencies; Gonzaga Institute for Hate Studies director Kristine Hoover calls for more meticulous reporting given that roughly a fifth of U.S. agencies do not participate in the FBI's tracking program.

source.title: History
source.outlet: Kootenai County Task Force on Human Relations (organizational page)
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: The task force's own account of its 1981 founding after the harassment of a Jewish restaurant owner and a bi-racial family in Kootenai County, and of the 2022 arrest of 31 Patriot Front members headed to confront a Pride event the group had helped provide security for; the page quotes Coeur d'Alene's police chief saying investigators had no doubt the group's U-Haul would have reached the event had officers not intervened.

source.title: About
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: The Coeur d'Alene-based institute's account of its 1998 founding as the education arm of the Kootenai County Task Force, seeded by a Gregory C. Carr Foundation grant made possible after the task force's successful civil lawsuit against the Aryan Nations.

source.title: Gonzaga Studies Hate
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: A conservative higher-education watchdog group's skeptical assessment of Gonzaga's hate-studies program, questioning the academic rigor of treating “hate” as a field of study; included to represent critical commentary on the institute.

source.title: Hate Map
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: SPLC's interactive database tracking hate and antigovernment groups nationwide; the 2025 edition documented over 1,260 such groups, part of the annual count the organization has published since 1990.

source.title: SPLC report: Hate propaganda is outpacing hate groups
source.section: Human Rights and Anti-Hate Organizations in the Inland Northwest
source.description: Reports the number of tracked hate and antigovernment groups fell 8% in 2025 even as flyering incidents surged, with SPLC framing the shift as far-right politics moving “from extreme to establishment” rather than genuinely receding; notes SPLC itself faced a Justice Department indictment around the same time.

source.title: An Idaho State Rep Promoted an Anti-Pride Event. Six Weeks Later, 31 Extremists Arrived
source.section: Heather Scott and Idaho Panhandle Politics
source.description: Connects Idaho Rep. Heather Scott's book-banning event, at which she invited the far-right Panhandle Patriots motorcycle club to speak, to the Patriot Front arrests six weeks later; reports at least two of those arrested had ties to Matt Shea's church.

source.title: North Idaho Rep. Heather Scott reaps the glory — and the consequences — of being one of Matt Shea’s biggest allies
source.section: Heather Scott and Idaho Panhandle Politics
source.description: Long-form profile built around a 2016 “God and Country” gathering where Shea introduced Scott as Idaho's “finest legislator” shortly after militia member LaVoy Finicum was killed during the Malheur refuge occupation.

source.title: North Idaho Rep. Heather Scott defends white nationalists in Facebook post
source.section: Heather Scott and Idaho Panhandle Politics
source.description: Reports Scott's Facebook post, published the day after the deadly Charlottesville rally, arguing that “white nationalist” simply meant a Caucasian supporter of the Constitution; a University of Idaho sociologist and a Vanderbilt professor both call her definition false.

source.title: Heather Scott defends statements on white nationalism
source.section: Heather Scott and Idaho Panhandle Politics
source.description: Scott responds to the Spokesman-Review's coverage by sending a critical statement to the Bonner County Daily Bee, saying her post was meant to “promote conversation” rather than defend white nationalism.

source.title: Heather Scott
source.section: Heather Scott and Idaho Panhandle Politics
source.description: Background reference on Scott's legislative record, including the 2017 white-nationalism controversy and a separate incident in which she told a female colleague that women earn committee posts only if they “spread their legs.”

source.title: Idaho Freedom Caucus
source.section: Heather Scott and Idaho Panhandle Politics
source.description: Background reference on the ultra-conservative legislative caucus co-chaired by Scott, describing its right-wing-populist and paleoconservative orientation and its affiliation with the national State Freedom Caucus Network.

source.title: Ammon Bundy, People’s Rights Network Slapped with $50 Million Judgment in Defamation Suit
source.section: Ammon Bundy and the People's Rights Network
source.description: SPLC's account of the Idaho jury verdict against Bundy and his People's Rights Network for harassing a Boise hospital and its staff, noting the loss came without the regional antigovernment movement rallying behind him as it had during earlier standoffs.

source.title: Ammon Bundy ordered to pay $26 million to Idaho hospital, its CEO and 2 staff members
source.section: Ammon Bundy and the People's Rights Network
source.description: National coverage of the defamation verdict against Bundy, who rose to prominence leading the 2016 armed occupation of the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge in Oregon, over his campaign accusing a hospital of “child trafficking.”

source.title: Bundy, Rodriguez ordered to pay $52.5M for Idaho hospital harassment, jury rules
source.section: Ammon Bundy and the People's Rights Network
source.description: Nonprofit statehouse newsroom's detailed breakdown of the damages award, including testimony that a hospital employee installed home security cameras and restricted her children's movements after being targeted by the harassment campaign.

source.title: Shawn Vestal: Matt Shea out at church over schism with fellow ‘general’ Ken Peters, but abortion protests go on
source.section: Ken Peters, Patriot Church, and the Marble Community
source.description: Columnist Shawn Vestal traces the falling-out between Shea and Ken Peters, the pastor who had installed Shea as his successor at Spokane's Covenant Church in 2020 before rescinding the arrangement, and revisits Shea's ties to the Marble Community and Christian Identity currents.

source.title: Patriot Churches
source.outlet: World Religions and Spirituality Project (academic reference)
source.section: Ken Peters, Patriot Church, and the Marble Community
source.description: Academic profile of Ken Peters, who started Covenant Church at a Spokane motel in 1998 before launching the explicitly nationalist “Patriot Church” network in 2020, tracing its theological ties to New Apostolic Reformation currents.

source.title: Seeking power in Jesus’ name: Trump sparks a rise of ‘Patriot Churches’
source.section: Ken Peters, Patriot Church, and the Marble Community
source.description: Profiles Peters directly, including his account of handing his Spokane congregation to Shea and his description of receiving a $20,000 donation from a Tennessee pastor to help launch the first Patriot Church.

source.title: Former Spokane mayor Woodward suing the city for $10 million
source.section: Nadine Woodward
source.description: Recaps the underlying August 2023 event — held indoors due to nearby wildfire smoke — at which Woodward appeared onstage with Feucht and Shea shortly before losing her re-election bid to Lisa Brown. Reported the same week Woodward's formal $10 million lawsuit was filed, following an earlier tort claim in April.

source.title: Spokane council approves another $650,000 to fight six lawsuits on Monday
source.section: Nadine Woodward
source.description: Reports two of six active lawsuits stem from the Woodward/Feucht dispute and two from firefighters fired for refusing COVID-19 vaccination under Woodward's tenure; notes Shea compared LGBTQ+ rights to the nearby wildfires while introducing Woodward onstage.

source.title: Statement on Feucht Lawsuit Dismissal
source.section: Nadine Woodward
source.description: The city's own statement on a Spokane County Superior Court ruling dismissing Feucht's claims on immunity grounds, quoting Mayor Lisa Brown and council leadership welcoming the outcome.

source.title: Pacifica Helps Spokane Defeat First Amendment Lawsuit by Christian Nationalist Preacher Sean Feucht
source.section: Nadine Woodward
source.description: The city's outside law firm details Judge Rachelle Anderson's ruling that the council's resolution carried no punitive or censorial effect and did not burden Feucht's speech or religious exercise, rejecting all of his claims.

source.title: City of Spokane facing new lawsuit from far-right pastor and musician
source.section: Nadine Woodward
source.description: Coverage of Feucht's original 2024 filing, detailing which council members were named as defendants and how each voted on the 2023 resolution that prompted the suit.

source.title: Elected officials condemn ‘armed vigilantes’ attending Spokane protests
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: Mayor Woodward, the full City Council, and several state legislators sign a joint statement condemning armed groups outside downtown businesses; Auntie's Bookstore owner John Waite publicly asks that they stop appearing outside his store.

source.title: Police should rein in assembly of armed militias, Spokane City Council proposal says
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: Details a council proposal invoking a state law against private militias parading with firearms; names Three Percenters member Jered Bonneau, who said his group's May 31 presence downtown was meant to “render aid.”

source.title: Not welcome here: City Council wants end to militia gatherings in Spokane
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: The council approves a nonbinding resolution asking police to intervene against armed militia gatherings; the Downtown Spokane Partnership disputes rumors it had supported the armed presence.

source.title: After a legal disagreement, Spokane City Council may take another step against militias
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: Reports the county prosecutor found the state's militia law difficult to enforce, prompting the city to consider incorporating the ban into municipal code so violations could be prosecuted locally.

source.title: Group of 16 Spokane-area leaders condemn ‘armed vigilantes’ at protests
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: Sixteen elected officials, including the full council, the mayor, and school board members, sign a statement opposing armed presence at protests; downtown businesses including the Globe Bar and Kitchen separately distance themselves from the groups.

source.title: Armed presence in North Idaho towns questioned by some politicians, business owners
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: Sandpoint's mayor says armed protesters with ties to extremist militia groups were summoned by a Bonner County commissioner over an unverified threat; describes similar armed patrols responding to rumors across small Western towns.

source.title: Spokane business owners concerned about armed militia groups
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: Auntie's Bookstore owner John Waite says up to 50 armed individuals gathered downtown in a single night and asks the city to discourage open carry near businesses.

source.title: Downtown Spokane businesses speaking out against armed groups during protests
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: The Globe and Blind Buck, LGBTQ-friendly downtown bars, issue statements affirming support for Black Lives Matter and rejecting any association with the armed groups that had gathered in their parking lot.

source.title: Armed people at Spokane protests criticized by politicians
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: National wire-style coverage of the joint statement from Spokane's council, mayor, and state legislators condemning armed vigilante presence at protests.

source.title: Spokane Mayor sets curfew for part of downtown for second night
source.section: Armed Militia Presence at the 2020 Spokane Protests
source.description: Police Chief Craig Meidl says Proud Boys, Antifa, and militia members were all present amid downtown chaos, while Sheriff Knezovich separately says Proud Boys did not cause damage and that militia members left when asked.

source.title: Cathy McMorris Rodgers, Russ Fulcher say they will contest Electoral College results as ‘civil war’ divides GOP
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Reports McMorris Rodgers's plan to object to certifying Biden's win in a joint session of Congress, part of a rift among congressional Republicans amplifying unproven fraud claims that judges, election officials, and Trump's own attorney general had all rejected.

source.title: Cathy McMorris Rodgers to object to Electoral College count
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: McMorris Rodgers frames her planned objection as examining election-integrity questions rather than overturning the result; Gov. Jay Inslee publicly calls the move a betrayal of the Constitution that will be remembered as “a mark of dishonor.”

source.title: Cathy McMorris Rodgers flips, backs Biden certification after Trump supporters storm Capitol
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Reports McMorris Rodgers's reversal mid-crisis, calling for a “peaceful transfer of power” as the Capitol riot unfolded, after having told the Spokesman-Review a day earlier that she intended to object.

source.title: In reversal after pro-Trump mob storms Capitol, McMorris Rodgers votes to certify election results; Pence declares Biden winner
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Details the chaotic overnight session in which McMorris Rodgers and a handful of other Republicans reversed planned objections after the riot, while roughly half of House Republicans still voted to challenge results in at least one state.

source.title: Congress certifies Biden’s win with more GOP support after Capitol breach
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Notes McMorris Rodgers was one of only two House Republicans who had planned to object to both the Arizona and Pennsylvania results but ultimately voted against both challenges after the riot.

source.title: Republican congresswoman will no longer support objections to electoral votes
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Live-blog entry quoting McMorris Rodgers's statement that the day's events were “disgraceful and un-American” and urging Trump to condemn the violence, alongside her explanation that her original objection concerned election-procedure changes rather than the outcome itself.

source.title: Rep. Cathy Anne McMorris Rodgers [R-WA5, 2005-2024]
source.section: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
source.description: Nonpartisan legislative-tracking reference summarizing McMorris Rodgers's two decades representing Washington's 5th district and her committee leadership roles.

source.title: Rep. Michael Baumgartner already faces seven challengers as year begins
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Notes one Democratic challenger, veteran Bajun Mavalwalla, is the father of a man arrested during a June 2025 ICE protest in Spokane; Baumgartner had won his 2024 open-seat race with more than 60% of the vote.

source.title: Congressman Michael Baumgartner met with opposition at town hall in Spokane
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: A Whitworth University town hall draws sustained pushback over Baumgartner's support for the Trump administration; Baumgartner says afterward his next town hall may be conducted by phone instead.

source.title: Big money, dark money, union money: The cash trying to win Washington’s 5th Congressional district seat
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Reports a surge of outside spending, including opaque super PAC money, defending Baumgartner ahead of the August 2026 primary against a crowded field of challengers.

source.title: Baumgartner meets with defense contractors, real estate agents in Spokane stop
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Covers a 12-county district tour stop in which Baumgartner fields sometimes-skeptical questions from realtors and defense contractors about state and local policy he does not directly control.

source.title: Michael Baumgartner
source.section: Michael Baumgartner
source.description: Background reference on Baumgartner's prior service as Spokane County treasurer and state senator, his unsuccessful 2012 U.S. Senate run against Maria Cantwell, and his 2024 election to succeed McMorris Rodgers.

source.title: Greater Idaho movement wants a seat at the table
source.section: Greater Idaho and Secession Movements
source.description: Nonprofit statehouse newsroom's assessment of renewed legislative pushes for a border-change study task force, framing the movement as a symptom of geographic polarization rather than its cause.

source.title: Map shows Oregon counties voting to join ‘Greater Idaho’
source.section: Greater Idaho and Secession Movements
source.description: Reports Crook County's vote made it the 13th Oregon county to endorse the border-change proposal, with organizers arguing rural conservative areas are dominated by the state's liberal-leaning western cities.

source.title: Conservative portion of blue state looking to break off and join neighboring red state
source.section: Greater Idaho and Secession Movements
source.description: Quotes Greater Idaho executive director Matt McCaw arguing voters' wishes should be honored via a legislative border compact, while noting Idaho's and Oregon's governors both declined to comment on the proposal.

source.title: The campaign to split Oregon in two: ‘We want to be governed by Idaho’
source.section: Greater Idaho and Secession Movements
source.description: Update noting the counties that back the plan voted heavily for Trump in the most recent presidential election even as statewide Oregon government remains Democratic-controlled.

source.title: Eastern Oregon residents pass ‘Greater Idaho’ measure
source.section: Greater Idaho and Secession Movements
source.description: Coverage of Crook County's vote, quoting the movement's argument that the 163-year-old Oregon-Idaho border no longer matches the region's cultural divide.

source.title: Greater Idaho movement
source.section: Greater Idaho and Secession Movements
source.description: Reference summary comparing the Greater Idaho proposal to historical U.S. border changes like the Dakota Territory split, noting most analysts consider the plan unlikely to ultimately succeed.

source.title: Turning Point USA founder visited Inland Northwest months before shooting death in Utah
source.section: Turning Point USA and Campus Conservative Activism
source.description: Notes Turning Point USA chapters exist at WSU, the University of Idaho, Eastern Washington University, Gonzaga, Whitworth, North Idaho College, and elsewhere regionally following founder Charlie Kirk's assassination at a Utah campus event.

source.title: Turning Point USA Whitworth and Gonzaga chapters host Spokane vigil for Charlie Kirk
source.section: Turning Point USA and Campus Conservative Activism
source.description: About a thousand people gather in Riverfront Park for a vigil organized by the two campus chapters; Gonzaga's chapter president says he hopes Kirk's death sparks a spiritual revival.

source.title: Turning Point USA chapters grapple with founder Charlie Kirk’s sudden death
source.section: Turning Point USA and Campus Conservative Activism
source.description: Whitworth chapter president Bree Pollack describes the club as a space where conservative students can speak without fear of social backlash, a theme she says felt more urgent after Kirk's death.

source.title: GU administration approves Turning Point USA chapter on campus
source.section: Turning Point USA and Campus Conservative Activism
source.description: Reports Gonzaga's dean of student development overruled a student-government committee's recommendation against approving the club, citing concerns the committee raised about the group's national affiliation.

source.title: Turning Point USA chapters at Whitworth, building conservative community
source.section: Turning Point USA and Campus Conservative Activism
source.description: Founding members describe chartering Whitworth's chapter in November 2022 to give conservative and libertarian students a space to discuss politics without fear of social consequences.

source.title: Libraries amplify ‘freedom to read in Spokane’ and feature challenged titles for ‘banned books week’
source.section: Book Bans and Library Censorship Debates
source.description: Spokane Public Library displays frequently challenged titles for Banned Books Week; notes the American Library Association tracked over 400 nationwide challenges to more than 1,100 titles between January and August that year.

source.title: ‘A tool to control the thoughts and actions of people’: New Washington law seeks to stop book bans
source.section: Book Bans and Library Censorship Debates
source.description: Reports on new state legislation responding to a national wave of book challenges driven by conservative activist groups invoking “parental rights” rhetoric, part of a trend PEN America says has been fueled by state-level legislation elsewhere.

source.title: Spokane and Gonzaga libraries reflect on national Banned Books Week
source.section: Book Bans and Library Censorship Debates
source.description: A Spokane County Library District youth-collection librarian says most book challenges she receives target titles related to social justice and LGBTQ+ topics, though some come from liberal parents challenging different material.

source.title: As elections near, Spokane sees growing interest in ballot systems
source.section: Election Integrity and Ballot-Security Activity
source.description: Reports the Spokane County elections office fielded a surge of public-records requests for 2020 election documents and saw increased public interest in equipment-testing procedures ahead of the 2022 midterms.

source.title: GOP groups organize Washington ballot box surveillance efforts
source.section: Election Integrity and Ballot-Security Activity
source.description: Covers Republican-organized efforts to monitor ballot drop boxes around the state, part of a wider election-security movement active in Spokane County.

source.title: Spokane County touts election transparency methods in place for midterms
source.section: Election Integrity and Ballot-Security Activity
source.description: County Auditor Vicky Dalton highlights an online ballot-tracking tool and new cameras monitoring the ballot-processing center's entrances, measures introduced partly in response to public skepticism about election security.

source.title: Spokane Pride Parade and Festival, and accompanying protests, will proceed unfazed by Wednesday’s tensions
source.section: Spokane Pride and Counter-Protest Activity
source.description: Previews a weekend combining Spokane Pride, a local “No Kings” rally, and a separate Sean Feucht event, days after an unrelated anti-ICE protest escalated into a citywide curfew; Pride organizers say they are well-prepared for possible spillover tension.

source.title: ‘A deeper sense of love’: Thousands celebrate pride in Spokane days after mass protests erupted
source.section: Spokane Pride and Counter-Protest Activity
source.description: Attendees describe feeling their celebration was intertwined with broader anxieties about immigration enforcement and LGBTQ+ rights under the current presidential administration.

source.title: Things to know going into Spokane’s weekend of planned protests and events
source.section: Spokane Pride and Counter-Protest Activity
source.description: Reports several Pride vendors withdrew citing security concerns, and that right-wing Facebook groups in North Idaho circulated posts urging members planning to counter-protest to practice firearm safety discipline.

source.title: Spokane council to consider mirroring LGBT+ protections; one member proposes protest amendments
source.section: Spokane Pride and Counter-Protest Activity
source.description: A council member proposes amendments to a proposed local LGBTQ+ protections ordinance framed around protecting religious and moral objectors, prompting debate over how far such carve-outs should extend.

source.title: More than 10,000 pack downtown for ‘No Kings’ protest
source.section: Spokane Pride and Counter-Protest Activity
source.description: Describes a large anti-Trump march that drew relatively few counter-protesters, one of whom carried a Confederate flag she described as representing “old-style America” rather than a racial statement.

source.title: Spokane Pride organizers prepare for protesters at annual Pride Parade
source.section: Spokane Pride and Counter-Protest Activity
source.description: Organizers describe de-escalation training for volunteers and a marching band deployed to drown out protesters' amplified sound, following a spate of Pride-mural vandalism incidents in the weeks before the parade.

source.title: Three Spokane defendants arrested after last June’s ICE protest hope a federal jury sees no conspiracy
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Previews the federal trial of three protesters charged after a June 2025 demonstration outside ICE's Spokane facility, where crowds gathered after former council president Ben Stuckart, the legal guardian of one detained asylum seeker, called for a peaceful sit-in.

source.title: Spokane police waited hours to respond to the ICE protest, upsetting federal agents. Here’s why
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Reconstructs the timeline of the June 2025 protest, in which around 20 demonstrators initially sat, sang, and passed out water in front of a bus meant to transport detained immigrants to Tacoma before the standoff escalated.

source.title: Spokane protest against ICE leads to 30 arrests, reports reveal
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Newly released body-camera footage and more than 200 pages of police reports detail the arrests of 30 people, including Stuckart, and SPD's transfer of seized protester cellphones to the FBI.

source.title: 3 Spokane ICE protesters found guilty in conspiracy case
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: A federal jury convicts military veteran Bajun Mavalwalla II and two co-defendants, known locally as the “Spokane Three,” of conspiracy to impede ICE agents, the first such case in the Eastern District of Washington.

source.title: Spokane Anti-ICE Activists Convicted of Federal Charges
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: A conservative-leaning outlet's account of the trial, describing the crowd's blocking of gates and vehicles as coordinated obstruction regardless of the protesters' political motivations; included to represent a right-of-center framing of the case.

source.title: Meet Bajun Mavalwalla, Veteran Convicted for ICE Protest in Unprecedented Use of Conspiracy Charges
source.section: ICE, Immigration Enforcement, and the Ben Stuckart Case
source.description: Mavalwalla, a U.S. military veteran, says he rejected a plea deal because it would have required falsely admitting to assault; the segment situates the Spokane case within a broader pattern of federal conspiracy charges against ICE protesters nationally.

source.title: Former state Rep. Matt Shea takes part in rescue of 62 orphans from Ukrainian city now ravaged by bombs, but some are questioning Shea's actions and children's future
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Shea says he helped move 62 children and two caregivers from a Mariupol orphanage to a small Polish town, working with a Texas-registered nonprofit called Loving Families and Homes for Orphans; a Chicago pediatrician on the scene says the paperwork looked legitimate, though he never saw it, and the U.S. State Department confirms it is reviewing volunteers' concerns.

source.title: Former WA Rep. Matt Shea, accused of domestic terrorism, working to secure adoptions for Ukrainian children in Poland
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Reports that Loving Families and Homes for Orphans is not registered as an adoption agency with Texas health authorities and is not accredited by the federal entity that oversees international adoptions; a local mayoral aide says Shea refused to explain his plans for the children or give his last name.

source.title: Former Washington state Rep. Matt Shea turns up in Poland, says he is helping orphans
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Notes local Polish officials, including the town's mayor, say they are unsure what legal authority Shea has to act as an adoption agent, and that the National Council for Adoption warns there is no way to confirm the children are actually orphans amid wartime chaos.

source.title: Concerns raised as former Wash. state Rep. Matt Shea tries to arrange Ukrainian adoptions
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Regional NPR-affiliate coverage noting adoption experts consider removing children from Ukraine for adoption a bad idea during active war, since family and orphan status is very difficult to verify under those conditions.

source.title: What The Heck Is U.S. Extremist Matt Shea Doing In Poland With 60 Ukrainian Kids?
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: National political outlet's roundup notes a Polish reporter's source claimed an American volunteer told local authorities the group intended to bring the children to the U.S., which Shea denied; flags that Loving Families and Homes for Orphans had also just been registered in Florida under a similar name.

source.title: An Ex-Lawmaker Accused of Terrorism Says He Rescued Ukrainian Kids
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Recaps Shea's 2019 domestic-terrorism finding as context, and reports that after initially barring Polish authorities from seeing the children, Shea relented; Shea posted that all adoptions and hosting programs were on hold, and international agencies including UNHCR and UNICEF said intercountry adoption was not appropriate during the war.

source.title: Matt Shea in Poland
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Independent Spokane outlet's investigation into Loving Families and Homes for Orphans' incorporation filings, finding the group was not a registered 501(c)(3), its website repeatedly failed to load, and a founding board member's listed address traced to rural land near Cheney, south of Spokane.

source.title: Ukrainian orphans with Matt Shea in Poland get a Polish legal guardian; children can't leave town for now, officials say
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: A Polish family court rules the children's Ukrainian orphanage director will share custody with a local Polish social-services official, and bars the children from leaving town except for medical emergencies, while the Lublin prosecutor's office decides within 30 days whether to open an investigation into Shea's conduct.

source.title: Ukrainian orphans with former WA state Rep. Matt Shea in Poland get legal guardians
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: The Ukrainian consul in Lublin says the children are safe and under Ukrainian-government supervision, and that roughly 200 Ukrainian orphans have left the country in total; Shea does not respond to requests for comment.

source.title: Polish authorities won't investigate Matt Shea following allegations of human trafficking
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: The District Prosecutor's Office in Lublin, Poland, declines to open a formal investigation into Shea's role in bringing the children to Poland; the piece notes that had Polish authorities proceeded, potential charges could have involved human trafficking tied to an illegal adoption, though none were ultimately filed.

source.title: 'This was a positive way for Evangelicals to rebrand themselves' — the troubles of Matt Shea, Ukraine and international adoptions
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Interview with Spokesman-Review reporter Eli Francovich, who describes finding that some of Loving Families and Homes for Orphans' website text had been copied from a different, unrelated hosting organization; situates the episode within a broader pattern of ethically fraught evangelical involvement in international adoption.

source.title: A Ukrainian Boy Spent a Month on a New York Family's Farm; They're Putting Their Trust in Matt Shea to Get Him Back
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Follows a specific New York family whose Ukrainian foster son, evacuated from the same Mariupol orphanage, ended up in Shea's group in Poland after their unrelated hosting arrangement was upended by the war, illustrating how Shea's operation intersected with existing, unrelated adoption cases already in process.

source.title: American Pastor Is Pissed That His Ukrainian Adoption Program Is Going Badly
source.section: Matt Shea and the Ukrainian Orphans Controversy
source.description: Opinion-inflected national coverage highlighting a direct contradiction: Shea claimed to be in Poland with the Kazimierz Dolny mayor's consent, but the mayor said it was in fact Shea who had asked to come, not the other way around.

source.title: Local developer releases video suggesting cure for downtown Spokane crime
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Developer Larry Stone releases “Curing Spokane,” a video modeled on Seattle's “Seattle Is Dying,” proposing a larger county jail, more downtown policing, relocating the STA transit plaza underground, and more parking; released three months before the Woodward-Stuckart mayoral election, with Woodward praising it and Stuckart criticizing its tone.

source.title: Developers offer mixed views on video's proposed 'cure' for Spokane
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Follow-up gathers reaction from other Spokane developers; Center for Justice founder Rick Sheehan argues the video's proposed jail expansion sidesteps the more complicated underlying issues of addiction and homelessness rather than addressing them.

source.title: Local advocates raise concerns with 'Curing Spokane' documentary
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Jewels Helping Hands founder Julie Garcia says the video overdramatizes street conditions and misrepresents some formerly homeless people shown as current drug users, arguing Spokane needs a “helping hand,” not a “cure.”

source.title: Spokane needs compassion and social justice, not a 'cure'
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: An urbanist blogger's rebuttal argues the county's own point-in-time count attributes most local homelessness to family breakdown and economic hardship rather than crime, and notes Stone's own developments have received public subsidy even as his video frames the unhoused as a public cost.

source.title: Spokane City Council approves zoning change to allow shelters, 'community services' in heavy industrial zones
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: The council temporarily rezones heavy-industrial land so Mayor Woodward's administration can pursue a shelter in a vacant East Trent Avenue warehouse, the building that becomes the Trent Resource and Assistance Center (TRAC).

source.title: 'I don't think it's ready': Proposed Spokane homeless shelter hits snag after zoning change fails to move forward
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: An earlier version of the East Trent Avenue zoning change first fails at the council, with the city not yet having secured a lease with building owner and developer Larry Stone — the same Larry Stone behind “Curing Spokane” three years earlier.

source.title: Spokane Council signals intent to purchase East Trent Avenue homeless shelter
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: The council votes 5-2 to pursue buying the TRAC warehouse outright from Stone's LLC, which had purchased it in March 2022 for $3.5 million; two council members, Michael Cathcart and Jonathan Bingle, vote no over long-term fiscal-sustainability concerns, and Woodward opposes expanding the city's real-estate portfolio.

source.title: Business owners blast Spokane City Council plan to relocate House of Charity
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: A West Central business owner's mass email to councilmembers and legislators argues concentrated shelters are harming small businesses and low-income neighbors who lack security systems, and calls for removing homeless facilities from downtown and its surrounding area; the city frames the relocation as decentralizing services rather than expanding them.

source.title: Controversy brews over Brown administration's transitional housing proposal
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Mayor Lisa Brown's administration works with Catholic Charities to move House of Charity out of downtown and with Compassionate Addiction Treatment (CAT) to relocate from Second and Division, as part of a broader shift from congregate shelters like TRAC toward a “scattered site” model; a proposed transitional-housing site at the Carlyle Hotel draws opposition from conservative councilmembers and downtown businesses.

source.title: Blowback to half-formed homeless project in Spokane portends murky path to a plan
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Catholic Charities CEO Rob McCann confirms a since-abandoned attempt to buy the Carlyle Hotel for transitional housing, part of a plan to move away from large congregate shelters; McCann says downtown “is terribly overwhelming small businesses — they're leaving,” while West Hills residents separately renew objections recalling their reaction to the nonprofit's earlier Catalyst Project.

source.title: 'It's not getting any better': Spokane businesses near homeless shelters want change
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Family-owned businesses near the Salvation Army's Way Out shelter describe needles and waste on their property and say conditions improved somewhat after the shelter shifted from low-barrier emergency use to a bridge-housing model; owners say they fear the city adding more low-barrier shelter space nearby.

source.title: Spokane opens new addiction recovery homeless shelter, partially replaces beds for families
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Compassionate Addiction Treatment (CAT) opens a recovery-focused shelter after facing years of opposition from developers, including Larry Stone, who blamed the nonprofit for disorder near its former Second and Division location; CAT's director rejects that characterization, saying neighborhood conditions had instead interfered with the group's own mission.

source.title: Spokane unveils plan to tackle crime downtown after months of pleas from community
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: The city announces its CORE downtown-safety plan, adding a police behavioral-health unit and fire department outreach team, after Spokesman-Review reporting found overdose deaths rose 18% locally even as they fell nationally, and a KHQ poll found 77% of residents considered downtown “Absolutely” dangerous.

source.title: Despite criticism of the city's handling of homelessness, data shows citations are up
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: City data show unlawful-camping citations roughly sextupled and pedestrian-interference citations more than doubled year-over-year, contradicting claims from some politicians and business groups that enforcement had lapsed.

source.title: Spokane re-criminalizing homelessness has had quick impact on the street
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Two weeks after the city toughened its public-camping and sidewalk-obstruction laws, business owners including Frank's Diner co-owner Robin Bernart describe reduced visible homelessness downtown, while people still sleeping outside say the citations mainly push them to less visible, less safe locations rather than into services.

source.title: Leaders tout progress in Spokane's new approach to homelessness
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: City officials describe a pivot toward enforcement-backed outreach after an earlier service-first ordinance drew sustained criticism from business owners and residents who said it lacked teeth to address safety concerns.

source.title: Saving Spokane: The Homeless Crisis Now
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Retrospective from the 2021 city-hall protests and Camp Hope encampment through the current scattered-site model; First Avenue Coffee owner Doyle Wheeler says he fears customers will leave again “and never come back” if downtown conditions worsen, while Mayor Lisa Brown says the city has “turned a corner.”

source.title: Locals only rated quality of life in Spokane area as 3.3 out of 10. Here's what else they said in new poll
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: A Greater Spokane Incorporated survey finds 75% of respondents don't feel safe downtown at night even though 62% feel safe there generally; the same piece notes downtown business openings have outpaced closures every year since the pandemic except 2024.

source.title: 2025 Policy Platform
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: The downtown business association's own policy document argues that concentrating shelters, low-barrier housing, and services in one part of the city makes that area “unsafe, including for the people these facilities are intended to serve,” and calls for regionally distributing homelessness services rather than concentrating them downtown.

source.title: New Data Dashboard to Increase Understanding of Homelessness System
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: The city, county, Spokane Valley, and the regional health district launch a shared public dashboard drawing on the Homeless Management Information System, intended to let residents and lawmakers track shelter capacity and program outcomes directly rather than relying on competing anecdotal claims.

source.title: Human trafficking industry growing in Spokane
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: Jonah Project founder Aaron Tilbury says homelessness is a major risk factor traffickers exploit, citing national statistics that one in five homeless children will be trafficked and a third solicited within 48 hours of becoming homeless; frames trafficking as preying on housing instability rather than attributing it to any specific shelter or shelter policy.

source.title: A Survey of Human Trafficking in the Spokane Region
source.outlet: Intercommunity Peace & Justice Center (regional nonprofit report)
source.section: Downtown Business Impact, Shelter Siting, and Homelessness Policy
source.description: A social-justice nonprofit's regional survey, compiled from interviews with local service agencies, describes Spokane as a historical entry point for teenage sex trafficking and catalogs case summaries in which homelessness, runaway status, and drug dependence recur as vulnerabilities traffickers exploited — documenting elevated risk among people already homeless rather than a causal link to shelter siting or policy.

source.title: Once again the Spokane River has run dry — this time two weeks earlier than before
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: For the second year running, a 1.5-mile stretch between Barker and Sullivan roads loses all surface water — two weeks earlier than 2025 — after Post Falls Dam reduced releases to protect Lake Coeur d'Alene levels; Spokane Riverkeeper's Jule Schultz says the seepage rate into the aquifer has roughly doubled over 20 years for reasons that remain unclear, and that the dry stretch is now “functionally dead.”

source.title: Experts raise concerns after parts of Spokane River lose all surface water for second year
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Spokane Riverkeeper says the 2026 dewatering is unfolding faster than in 2025 and frames it as one more consequence of a hotter, drier regional climate already visible in the summer's wildfires.

source.title: Spokane River reaches potential water record lows after 'perfect storm' of conditions
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: The river's first-ever documented complete dewatering between Barker and Sullivan roads; Riverkeeper staff say Spokane-area water use is well above the national per-capita average, and that high summer lawn-watering demand pulls river water into the aquifer rather than the other way around along this stretch.

source.title: Sections of Spokane River are running dry
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: A 33-year Spokane Valley resident says he has never before seen the riverbed at Flora Trailhead completely exposed; Avista says it will increase Post Falls Dam discharge after Labor Day, which is expected to restore flow.

source.title: 'How people use water matters': Spokane Riverkeeper urges conservation as parts of Spokane River run dry
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Riverkeeper staff say the dewatered stretch immediately threatens fish, wildlife and habitat, and note a relatively small reduction in outdoor irrigation time — about 10% — could meaningfully help the specific reach that depends on surface flow.

source.title: A portion of the Spokane River ran dry last week. Can we do more to conserve water?
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: City council member Kitty Klitzke, who has 15 years of environmental-advocacy experience, says she has never known the river to run dry like this; the piece notes average Spokane-area water use is roughly double the national per-capita rate, comparing unfavorably even to Arizona and Nevada.

source.title: The Summer The River Disappeared: Documenting the Spokane River's Dry Stretch
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: First-person account from Riverkeeper staff describing a mile and a half of completely dry riverbed, the smell of rotting fish and aquatic plants, and a great blue heron picking off bass and crayfish trapped in the shrinking pools — the organization's own record of the 2025 event.

source.title: Spokane River Is Running Dry — Sign the Petitions to Protect Its Flows
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: The advocacy group's campaign page argues the Post Falls Dam's operating rules, set through a federal relicensing process that only recurs every 40-50 years, were never designed to adapt to a changing climate, and is petitioning regulators to reopen that process ahead of schedule.

source.title: A toxic past and present on the Spokane River
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Traces PCB contamination from Cold War-era industrial discharge into the Spokane River, including Monsanto-linked lawsuits several West Coast cities have joined to recoup cleanup costs, and profiles a Lands Council-run bioremediation project using walnut-shell filtration and student-tested microbes to break the chemicals down.

source.title: EPA proposes PCBs cleanup plan for Spokane River
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: The EPA opens public comment on a Total Maximum Daily Load, or pollution budget, for PCBs across 100 miles of the Spokane and Little Spokane rivers, targeting both remaining industrial sources and the electrical equipment manufactured before the 1979 PCB ban that is still in use today.

source.title: Collaborating for cleaner water: The next step for the Spokane River
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: The state agency notes wastewater-treatment upgrades have physically removed PCBs from effluent, but that EPA denied its 2024 petition to tighten federal limits on the trace “inadvertent” PCBs still legally present in consumer products, which continue reaching the river through stormwater.

source.title: Wastewater PCBs
source.outlet: City of Spokane (public works program page)
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: The city's own accounting of its PCB-reduction program under its Integrated Clean Water Plan, noting the Spokane River and Lake Spokane remain on the state's official list of impaired waterbodies for PCBs even as mandated projects reduce discharge.

source.title: Bunker Hill mine restarts, raising pollution concerns for Lake Coeur d'Alene
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Bunker Hill Mining Corp. ships its first concentrate in 45 years from the historic Silver Valley mine, reviving fears of renewed heavy-metal contamination reaching Lake Coeur d'Alene at the site that triggered the second-largest Superfund designation in U.S. history.

source.title: Bunker Hill Mining & Metallurgical Complex — Superfund Site Profile
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: The EPA's own site summary describing a century of mining and smelting that spread lead across the Coeur d'Alene River Basin, a $180 million settlement with Hecla Mining funding ongoing cleanup, and a caution that a full remedy will take decades.

source.title: Challenges — Lake Management
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: The Coeur d'Alene Tribe's own account of the Bunker Hill Superfund site's scope — several thousand contaminated acres from a century of mining discharge — and of the tribe's role, alongside EPA and Idaho regulators, in managing the lake it has stewarded for centuries.

source.title: The EPA Can't Wait to Reopen the Mine That Poisoned North Idaho
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Long-form investigation into the Bunker Hill Mine's legacy — 75 million tons of toxic sludge deposited in Lake Coeur d'Alene — and EPA's contested push to encourage new mining in the same Silver Valley canyons even as the decades-long federal cleanup continues.

source.title: Lead Heads and a Toxic Timebomb: The Bunker Hill Superfund Site
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Academic public-history entry noting the Coeur d'Alene Tribe has fought for decades for a decision-making role in cleanup planning, and that the lake itself was not formally added to the Superfund site until 2002, nearly 20 years after the surrounding basin.

source.title: Smoke Streams Across Eastern Washington
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Satellite imagery from NASA's Terra spacecraft shows wildfire smoke pouring across Spokane and into Idaho, Montana, and Canada in early August 2026, coinciding with Gov. Bob Ferguson's statewide wildfire emergency declaration and burn ban.

source.title: Nearby wildfires contributing to Spokane-area unsafe air conditions, local events postponed
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: Air quality in Liberty Lake hits a hazardous 351 rating; the city activates inclement-weather shelter beds for the homeless population, a protocol also triggered by extreme heat, and notes the last comparably bad smoke stretch was August 2023.

source.title: Thick wildfire smoke causes dangerous air quality in the Northwest
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: National weather outlet's coverage as smoke from the early-August 2026 Spokane wildfires spreads across Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Montana, with meteorologists noting prevailing winds are at least carrying the worst of it away from Seattle and Portland.

source.title: Preparing Washington's second largest city for wildfire season
source.outlet: University of Washington Dept. of Environmental & Occupational Health Sciences
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: UW researchers partner with Gonzaga University on a $1.1 million EPA grant to make Spokane “smoke ready,” citing the 2023 wildfires that burned more than 200,000 acres and destroyed roughly 360 homes as the impetus for building longer-term public-health infrastructure around smoke exposure.

source.title: Explosive wildfire activity spreads smoke across Washington
source.section: Environmental and Ecological Hardship in the Spokane Region
source.description: State agency update describing hundreds of structures burned in Spokane and unhealthy-to-very-unhealthy air quality spreading statewide as multiple large fires burn simultaneously with little relief in sight for firefighters.

source.title: New more powerful license plate cameras may soon be scanning Inland Northwest vehicles
source.section: Flock Cameras, License Plate Readers, and Mass Surveillance
source.description: Spokane County considers Flock Safety automated license-plate readers that also log vehicle make and color searchable for 30 days; a privacy advocate identified as Lee argues the retention period itself constitutes unacceptable surveillance, while a sheriff's office lieutenant says the system is a less-biased way to gather evidence.

source.title: Flock investigation
source.section: Flock Cameras, License Plate Readers, and Mass Surveillance
source.description: Independent Spokane outlet's investigative series finds nearly 100 Flock cameras operating across Spokane County alone, part of a network covering as many as 80 Washington cities, constantly logging every passing vehicle rather than only those suspected of a crime; the series includes public-records data the outlet obtained on what other agencies have searched the shared database for.

source.title: The State of Surveillance in Spokane
source.section: Flock Cameras, License Plate Readers, and Mass Surveillance
source.description: Follow-up reporting finds Airway Heights' Walmart Foundation-funded camera network shares data with both Liberty Lake police and the Spokane County Sheriff's Office; the city of Spokane itself says it has no current plans to purchase a Flock system after a state grant meant to fund one lapsed, though SPD can still access some regional camera data through partner agencies' logins.

source.title: Stanwood reactivates Flock cameras as Spokane County joins Pierce County in shutting them down
source.section: Flock Cameras, License Plate Readers, and Mass Surveillance
source.description: Washington's new Driver Privacy Act (Senate Bill 6002) requires deleting most license-plate data within 21 days, bars collection near schools and immigration facilities, and restricts sharing with out-of-state or federal agencies; Spokane County shuts its cameras off entirely rather than reconfigure under the new rules, while other cities choose to comply and continue operating.

source.title: Spokane sheriff shuts down Flock cameras, cites SB 6002 risk
source.section: Flock Cameras, License Plate Readers, and Mass Surveillance
source.description: Coverage sympathetic to law enforcement's objections quotes a state lawmaker involved in the bill acknowledging Democrats crafted it partly out of concern the technology could be used to track immigrant communities or monitor abortion-clinic visitors, cases the piece argues didn't reflect how Spokane County had actually used the system.

source.title: Spokane County Sheriff's Office Experiences Rapid Case Resolution with Real-time Intelligence & LPR for Every Roadway
source.section: Flock Cameras, License Plate Readers, and Mass Surveillance
source.description: The vendor's own promotional case study on its partnership with the Spokane County Sheriff's Office, framing years of budget constraints as the main reason the office waited to adopt license-plate-reader technology before eventually contracting with Flock.

source.title: Spokane Police: Man involved in shooting, standoff in downtown Spokane is dead
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: Dominic Shears, 39, is killed by police after a nearly five-hour standoff following a robbery at a Spokane Valley hotel where he and two accomplices had targeted a drug dealer under DEA and ATF surveillance; two other officers used pepper balls, flash bangs, and gas canisters before Shears exited his crashed van still armed and was fatally shot.

source.title: Prosecutor finds Spokane Police officers, deputy justified in Aug. 2022 shooting that ended standoff with robber who shot at police
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: The county prosecutor rules the shooting of Dominic Shears justified nearly two years later; his accomplices, Christopher Gooch and Christopher Jones, are separately sentenced to four years in state prison and more than five years in federal prison.

source.title: 2 Fairchild sergeants accused of stealing ammo from base after anti-government rhetoric posted online
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: John Sanger and Eric Eagleton are charged after an Inland Northwest Joint Terrorism Task Force investigation found Sanger tied to online posts calling for the Capitol to be seized by force weeks after the 2020 election, and recorded Eagleton describing routine theft of thousands of rounds from Fairchild's training section along with antisemitic views.

source.title: Deputies searching for Spokane Valley drive-by shooting suspects
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: No one is hurt after multiple shots are fired into an occupied East Trent apartment around 2:49 a.m.; the resident reports seeing a light-colored Honda SUV, possibly bearing an Idaho plate, leaving the scene.

source.title: Spokane Valley man arrested after threatening neighbors with gun prompts SWAT response
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: A 69-year-old man threatens to shoot neighbors doing yard work on North Greenacres Road, prompting a SWAT, K9, and crisis-negotiator response; a search after his arrest turns up two loaded pistols, two loaded shotguns, and a rifle.

source.title: Man shot twice at Spokane Valley house party
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: A party of roughly 15 people on Park Road erupts in gunfire after an unknown group arrives and an argument escalates; the wounded man is found blocks away, and witnesses who fled left behind cellphones but declined to identify anyone involved.

source.title: Two shot in Spokane Valley driveway shooting
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: Two people are shot multiple times in their own driveway near 8th and Havana after a group they exchanged words with opened fire; deputies believe the shooting was targeted and that suspects remain at large.

source.title: Spokane Valley home hit by gunfire for third time in under two years
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: A shooting on East 7th Avenue leaves a man hospitalized in stable condition; the same home was the site of a 2019 assault-related shooting and a fatal February 2020 shooting for which Brian Riley was later convicted of first-degree murder.

source.title: Spokane police shoot, kill domestic violence suspect in Logan neighborhood
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: Officers responding to a 5 a.m. domestic-violence call near Gonzaga University shoot and kill a man after an altercation involving a weapon; the woman and children in the home are unharmed and no officers are hurt.

source.title: Investigation finds Spokane man killed in 2022 police shooting pointed gun at officers
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: Nineteen months after Robert Bradley was killed while officers served a firearm-surrender and protection order in Hillyard, SPD releases bodycam footage and forensic findings — including a police round found lodged in Bradley's own pistol barrel — that a county review called proof he had aimed his weapon at officers; his fiancée later sues, calling it an ambush.

source.title: Spokane homeowner seeks compensation after police shooting leaves damage, blood in backyard
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: Colt Ward wakes to police shooting and killing Apple Tree Inn stabbing suspect Richard Sheppard in his backyard, then says the city offered no cleanup help beyond referrals to a grant program, leaving him to weigh filing an insurance claim over broken fencing and biohazard cleanup himself.

source.title: 'Something irreplaceable': Family mourns teen shot while at a friend's house
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: Thirteen-year-old Gavin Looper's mother and older brother describe the early-morning shooting that killed him after someone fired through a back door; police had not publicly identified a suspect as of the story's publication and had not responded to the outlet's requests for updated information.

source.title: The United States Attorney's Office and City of Spokane Announce Appointment of a Special Assistant United States Attorney to Prosecute Drug Trafficking in the City of Spokane
source.outlet: U.S. Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Washington (press release)
source.section: Individual Shootings and Violent Crime Incidents (2019-2026)
source.description: Spokane native Annika Tangvald is sworn in as a city-funded federal prosecutor dedicated to fentanyl and other narcotics cases, a position the city council unanimously funded in late 2024; Mayor Lisa Brown calls it a step toward holding traffickers accountable.

source.title: Spokane replaces downtown garbage cans it rented for $106,000 per year
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: The city removes solar-powered “smart” trash cans leased since 2018 from a Massachusetts company after learning residents routinely ignored the bins' “suggestion” to keep large items out, defeating the sensors meant to cut staffing costs; new owned bins cost just over $200,000 but are projected to save roughly $367,000 over five years.

source.title: 'Piece of sh-art': 4 News Now investigates problems with the 'eyesore' you paid for in Riverfront Park
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: The Stepwell sculpture, commissioned for more than $500,000 during the Riverfront Park makeover, has spent much of its existence closed off; internal emails obtained by the outlet show city staff privately referring to the graffiti-prone, cracking structure as an eyesore.

source.title: Getting There: North Spokane Corridor project beginning summer 2026 to be most expensive in Eastern Washington history
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: A single one-mile stretch of the freeway will cost $224 million and extend the elevated “road to nowhere” beside Spokane Community College; WSDOT's spokesman notes the decades-long project, planned since the 1950s and under construction since 2001, had long been a regional punchline before finally becoming visible.

source.title: North Spokane Corridor to steadily progress through 2026
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: Total project funding has grown to $1.9 billion, up from $1.5 billion the year before, attributed to inflation and labor and material costs; full completion of the 10.5-mile corridor is not expected until late 2030 or 2031.

source.title: Getting There: Work on North Spokane Corridor in 2026 lays groundwork for completion
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: Describes commissioned artwork built into the freeway itself near Spokane Community College — embossed concrete columns depicting feathers and balsamroot by Spokane artist Melissa Cole — plus a separate community survey soliciting input on additional artist Reinaldo Gil Zambrano's drawings for the pending I-90 tie-in segment.

source.title: WSDOT Case Study: US 395 North Spokane Corridor Murals
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: The formliner manufacturer's own marketing case study describes custom concrete murals — including a large “Running Horses” scene — engineered across two contractors and two production plants to meet WSDOT's durability and design standards for the freeway's retaining walls and overpasses.

source.title: North Spokane Corridor
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: Background reference noting the freeway's first cost estimate, in 1956, was $13 million — versus the $1.9 billion figure attached to the project seven decades later — and tracing the project's on-and-off planning history back through the 1960s and '70s.

source.title: State audit of Spokane's Community, Housing and Human Services finds conflicts of interest, mishandling of money
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: State auditors find the city department overseeing homeless-shelter and social-service contracts skipped required competitive-bidding steps for some agreements; Catholic Charities disputes the findings, saying no one at the organization named in the report was ever contacted by investigators.

source.title: State audit flags $170M in misstatements in Spokane under Brown's oversight
source.section: Public Spending Oddities and Accountability
source.description: A state audit finds Spokane misclassified and mistimed roughly $170 million across several funds, understating the general fund by $18.6 million alone; the city's finance chief attributes the errors to high turnover in accounting positions and says all findings have since been corrected.

source.title: Rep. Matt Shea won't resign, draws Trump impeachment comparison
source.outlet: KOMO News (via Seattle P-I's Joel Connelly)
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: After being expelled from the House GOP caucus, Shea compares his situation to Trump's, posting that it is a “sham investigation,” while House Minority Leader J.T. Wilcox calls for his resignation on social media and Shea keeps his seat since expulsion requires a two-thirds House vote.

source.title: Washington Legislator Matt Shea Accused Of 'Domestic Terrorism,' Report Finds
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: National coverage detailing the Rampart Group's findings that Shea planned three armed conflicts between 2014 and 2016 — the Bundy Ranch standoff, a 2015 armed blockade of a VA weapons seizure in Priest River, Idaho, and the Malheur refuge occupation — and that he met with Oath Keepers militia leaders at a Spokane restaurant to discuss weapons and snipers.

source.title: Kicking Matt Shea out of Washington's Legislature: Can it be done?
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Explains that expelling a sitting legislator requires a two-thirds House vote and has succeeded only once in state history (a 1933 statutory-rape case), and that a Guardian report on Shea's ties to the Christian Identity white-supremacist movement had already fueled resignation calls before the Rampart investigation concluded.

source.title: House investigation report
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: The Legislature's own archive of the Rampart Group's 108-page report and dozens of supporting exhibits — emails, Facebook posts, encrypted chat logs, police incident reports, and an audio recording of Shea at the Malheur occupation — documenting the underlying evidence cited throughout subsequent news coverage.

source.title: Rep. Matt Shea endorsed training children to fight in holy war
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Leaked emails show Shea connected Team Rugged organizer Patrick Caughran, who sought to train boys and young men for “Christian warfare” against Muslims using theology from a preacher who defended slavery, with far-right podcaster Jack Robertson; Sheriff Knezovich compares the youth-training group to the Hitler Youth.

source.title: GOP legislator Matt Shea coordinated anti-government land occupation in Oregon, investigators find
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: National coverage notes Shea once introduced legislation to split Washington into a gun- and church-friendly “Liberty State,” that Sheriff Knezovich said there was enough evidence to charge Shea with “domestic terrorism, if not treason,” and that Gov. Jay Inslee called the findings “disturbing” and “unacceptable.”

source.title: Matt Shea and the 'Biblical Basis for War': Team Rugged training report
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: The Guardian's original report on leaked emails connecting Shea to Team Rugged, a group offering youth paramilitary and religious-combat training in Marble, Washington; the story broke days before the Spokesman-Review's own follow-up reporting and directly prompted the state House to accelerate its Rampart Group investigation.

source.title: Washington state Republican distributes 'Biblical Basis for War' document
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: The Guardian's original report on Shea's four-page “Biblical Basis for War” manifesto, which called for a “Holy Army” to enforce biblical law and stated “if they do not yield – kill all males”; Sheriff Ozzie Knezovich told reporters the document was consistent with the ideology of the Christian Identity and Aryan Nations movements, not an academic sermon outline as Shea claimed.

source.title: Legislator pulled gun during road incident
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Years before the domestic-terrorism findings, Shea is cited for having a loaded, unpermitted handgun in his truck after pulling it during a road-rage dispute in downtown Spokane; the charge is dismissed after a year under a standard stipulated continuance.

source.title: Knezovich requests Republicans denounce Shea
source.section: Matt Shea
source.description: Three years before the domestic-terrorism report, Sheriff Knezovich publicly clashes with Shea for the first time, formally asking the county GOP to censure him after Shea suggested on his podcast that a sheriff's deputy was tied to a triple-murder suspect; Shea partially retracted the claim under pressure.

source.title: Woman dragged out of Kootenai County Republican town hall event in Coeur d'Alene: 'Please don't touch me'
source.section: Coeur d'Alene Town Hall Dragging Incident
source.description: Kootenai County Sheriff Bob Norris personally confronts Teresa Borrenpohl, a repeat Democratic legislative candidate, after she jeers speakers at a GOP town hall, then summons private security guards from Lear Asset Management who drag her from the auditorium as she screams; Coeur d'Alene's police chief and the sheriff publicly disagree over the incident's First Amendment implications.

source.title: Coeur d'Alene police recommend criminal charges for town hall security team
source.section: Coeur d'Alene Town Hall Dragging Incident
source.description: After a weekslong investigation, city police recommend battery and false-imprisonment charges against the private security guards involved, along with security-license violations, following the widely circulated video of Borrenpohl's removal.

source.title: Private security guards charged in Coeur d'Alene town hall dragging
source.section: Coeur d'Alene Town Hall Dragging Incident
source.description: Prosecutors file misdemeanor battery and false-imprisonment charges against four Lear Asset Management guards and a fifth private citizen; investigators also document a separate incident in which a guard is accused of touching another attendee's breast while forcibly restraining her.

source.title: Private Security Guards Charged After Woman Was Dragged Out of Chaotic Idaho Town Hall Meeting
source.outlet: The Associated Press (via U.S. News & World Report)
source.section: Coeur d'Alene Town Hall Dragging Incident
source.description: National wire coverage of the charges notes Borrenpohl filed a tort claim signaling her intent to sue Kootenai County, and that roughly 450 people attended the town hall hosted by the Kootenai County Republican Central Committee.

source.title: Witnesses react to lawsuit over Coeur d'Alene town hall where woman was dragged out
source.section: Coeur d'Alene Town Hall Dragging Incident
source.description: More than a year after her tort claim, Borrenpohl formally sues Sheriff Norris, Kootenai County GOP chair Brent Regan, and the security firm, alleging violations of her First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendment rights; witnesses say the case matters regardless of political viewpoint because it tests the public's right to attend and speak at government-adjacent forums.

source.title: Private security guards who dragged Idaho woman from town hall meeting hit with charges
source.section: Coeur d'Alene Town Hall Dragging Incident
